n: South Korea — Truth and Reconciliation Commission finds state responsible for overseas-adoption abuses
who: South Korean government; private adoption agencies (Wikipedia list cites Holt Children's Services, Eastern Social Welfare Society, Korea Social Service, Korea Welfare Services)
cover: The commission found the government neglected its duty to oversee agencies; children were falsely registered as orphans and identities were swapped when a child died before departure.
d: On 26 March 2025, after a two-year inquiry into petitions from 367 adoptees sent abroad between 1964 and 1999 to 11 countries, the commission found human rights violations in at least 56 cases. It found agencies sent set numbers of children each month to meet foreign agencies' demand, falsely registered children with known parents as orphans, did not properly obtain consent and failed to vet adoptive parents. It said the state treated overseas adoption as a cheap alternative to domestic welfare and recommended an official apology and ratification of the Hague Convention. President Lee Jae-myung apologised on 2 October 2025.

n: Nazi Germany — kidnapping of Polish and other children for Germanization (RuSHA trial)
place: Occupied Poland (Łódź region, Zamość and others)
who: SS Race and Settlement Main Office (RuSHA), Lebensborn e.V., SS
d: Nazi Germany seized children judged 'racially valuable' in occupied Poland and elsewhere, held them in Lebensborn and other homes and placed them with German families under new identities; DW reports estimates of up to 200,000 Polish children kidnapped and forcibly 'Germanized'. In the RuSHA trial (United States v. Ulrich Greifelt et al., Nuremberg Military Tribunal I), 14 leading officials of the SS Race and Settlement Main Office, Lebensborn and related bodies were charged with crimes including the kidnapping of 'racially valuable' children; charges were read on 10 October 1947, the trial ran from 20 October 1947 to 17 February 1948, and on 10 March 1948 the tribunal convicted 13 — Greifelt was sentenced to life — and acquitted one.

n: Cambodia — Lauryn Galindo adoption-fraud conspiracy; US moratorium 2001
who: US facilitator Lauryn Galindo and associates; Cambodian officials paid by facilitators
d: The US imposed a moratorium on Cambodian adoptions in late 2001 after fraudulent cases and raids by the Cambodian rights group LICADHO. Facilitator Lauryn Galindo arranged about 800 adoptions for US families in 1997–2001, more than half of all Cambodian adoptions; the US government said her business paid Cambodian mothers for babies. In 2004 she pleaded guilty to conspiracy to commit visa fraud and money laundering in 17 cases, admitting she falsified documents that erased children's identities (she denied trafficking), and faced an 18-month sentence. Some adoptive families later found their children had living relatives.

n: Guatemala — notary-run adoption trade to the US (1996–2007)
who: Private notaries (notarios), baby brokers, foster homes, officials
d: After the civil war ended in 1996, adoptions abroad rose each year, run almost entirely (about 98%) by private notaries who handled both sides without court review and charged $35,000 or more per child; 97% of children went to the US. CICIG's 2010 report studied 153 cases and found 78% violated the new law in some way. Guatemala passed a Hague-compliant law on 11 December 2007 and stopped new adoptions to the US from 1 January 2008; the US State Department announced on 9 January 2008 it would not allow new adoptions until procedures were compliant.

n: India — Preet Mandir, Pune: CBI case on inter-country adoption racket
who: Preet Mandir adoption agency; state officials
d: Preet Mandir placed 518 children in 2004–2006, most abroad, and Frontline reported in 2005 it handled about 7% of India's foreign adoptions while charging high 'donation' fees. CNN-IBN reported in December 2007 that the CBI had confirmed findings on illegal adoptions. On 18 May 2010 the CBI registered a case against a managing trustee and state officials over an alleged inter-country adoption racket.

n: Netherlands — Joustra committee: state failed to stop intercountry adoption abuses; all adoptions suspended
who: Dutch government (Justice ministry), licensed Dutch adoption intermediaries, intermediaries in sending countries
cover: The government revealed in February 2021 that its officials were aware of wrongdoing for years and had failed to intervene (BBC).
d: The Commission of Inquiry into Intercountry Adoption, set up in 2019 and chaired by Tjibbe Joustra, reported in February 2021 after a two-year investigation that found 'serious violations' in adoptions from countries including Sri Lanka, Indonesia, Bangladesh, Brazil and Colombia between 1967 and 1997/98, and concluded the Dutch government had for decades failed to prevent abuses and protect children's rights. The government suspended all intercountry adoptions with immediate effect on 8 February 2021. About 4,000 of the children were from Sri Lanka.

n: El Salvador — children disappeared by the armed forces during the civil war (Pro-Búsqueda)
who: Salvadoran armed forces
cover: The armed forces have not granted access to archives on disappeared children despite years of lobbying.
d: Pro-Búsqueda, founded in 1994, has documented close to a thousand children disappeared during the Salvadoran civil war, mostly by the armed forces; many were adopted through flawed procedures to the US, France, Spain, Italy and the Netherlands. On 1 March 2005 the Inter-American Court of Human Rights ruled on the 1982 disappearance of the Serrano Cruz sisters during the 'Guinda de Mayo' military operation. El Salvador created a National Search Commission for Disappeared Children in 2010.

n: Nigeria — Aba 'baby farm': 32 pregnant girls freed
who: Cross Foundation clinic proprietor
d: In late May 2011 Abia State police raided the Cross Foundation clinic in Aba and rescued 32 pregnant girls, mostly aged 15–17, allegedly held so their babies could be sold for illegal adoption or ritual use; four babies already sold were recovered. The proprietor was arrested, according to police commissioner Bala Hassan. Nigerian police had uncovered a network of 'baby farms' posing as orphanages in Enugu in 2008, and more were found in later years (five in 2013, eight in 2015 per Makinde et al.).

n: Chad — Zoé's Ark tries to fly 103 children to France (convicted 2007)
who: French charity L'Arche de Zoé (founder Éric Breteau)
d: In October 2007 members of the French charity Zoé's Ark were detained in Chad as they tried to fly 103 children to France; the charity said they were orphans from Sudan's Darfur region, but authorities found most were from Chad and not orphans. On 26 December 2007 a Chadian court convicted six French members of attempting to kidnap the children and sentenced them to eight years' forced labour, and ordered each to pay €60,000 to each of the 103 children; a Chadian and a Sudanese defendant got four years and two Chadians were acquitted. The six were transferred to France, and Chad's President Idriss Déby pardoned them at the end of March 2008.

n: Sweden — state inquiry into intercountry adoptions (report 2 June 2025)
who: Swedish state authorities and adoption organisations
d: Sweden's independent inquiry into intercountry adoptions issued its report on 2 June 2025 (nearly 1,600 pages), reviewing 65 years of adoption history and documenting numerous irregularities and illegalities of which state authorities had some knowledge. Sweden had already stopped adoptions from South Korea (AP, 2024). Sweden received 9,051 Korean children 1957–2005, and in January 1975 the Swedish ambassador urged South Korea to continue sending children after it tried to halt adoptions to Scandinavia.

n: Uruguay — Gelman v. Uruguay: baby taken from disappeared mother (Operation Condor)
who: Uruguayan Defense Information Service (SID); joint Argentine–Uruguayan commando under Operation Condor
cover: Uruguay's 1986 Expiry Law was used to close the investigation in 2003.
d: A pregnant 19-year-old Argentine detained in Buenos Aires in August 1976 was moved secretly to Montevideo, gave birth in a military hospital, and her baby was taken in December 1976 and left with a police officer's family, who raised her under another identity for 23 years. On 24 February 2011 the Inter-American Court of Human Rights found Uruguay responsible for enforced disappearance and suppression of the child's identity, and ruled the 1986 Expiry Law amnesty legally ineffective.

n: United States / UK — 'internet twins' sold twice through an online adoption broker
place: St Louis, Missouri; broker in El Cajon, California; twins taken to Wales
who: Internet agency A Caring Heart (broker in California)
d: In 2000–01 a California-based internet adoption broker placed six-month-old twin girls first with a Californian couple, who paid about £4,000 and were then persuaded to return them to the birth mother, and then with a couple from north Wales who paid about £8,200 and adopted them in Arkansas. After the Welsh couple publicised the purchase in January 2001, Prime Minister Tony Blair promised action against trading children for adoption, Flintshire council took the twins into care under an emergency protection order, and on 9 April 2001 the High Court ruled they should be returned to the US. The FBI searched the broker's home near San Diego on 14 March 2001. The case led to UK adoption reform, including penalties for bringing children into the UK for adoption without approval.

n: Jersey care system and Haut de la Garenne — Independent Jersey Care Inquiry
place: Haut de la Garenne, St Martin, Jersey
who: States of Jersey children's services; Haut de la Garenne children's home
cover: The inquiry found the authorities failed to build a culture of transparency, feeding perceptions of collusion and cover-up, and a 'small island culture' that was not countered.
d: The Independent Jersey Care Inquiry reported in July 2017 after hearing from about 450 people connected with Jersey's care system since 1945. It found the States of Jersey had been 'an ineffectual and neglectful substitute parent', that its child-welfare law was decades behind, and that some children in care might still be at risk. Haut de la Garenne, centre of the 2007–2010 police investigation Operation Rectangle, was described as a symbol of the turmoil and the inquiry recommended its buildings be demolished. Chief Minister Ian Gorst apologised: 'We failed children who needed our care.'

n: Islington Council children's homes, London
who: London Borough of Islington children's homes and foster placements (42 homes)
cover: A 2018 report by Sarah Morgan QC found that councillor Sandy Marks knew of abuse allegations before the Evening Standard published them in 1992; the council leadership publicly denied the newspaper's reports at the time.
d: Survivors say children in Islington's 42 children's homes and in foster care were abused between the 1960s and 1990s; the Evening Standard exposed abuse in the homes in 1992. A 2018 independent report by Sarah Morgan QC into former councillor Sandy Marks found evidence linking her to the 'Fallen Angels' group (which she denies) but no evidence it affected her council duties or that she learned of organised abuse. Islington later set up a support payment scheme for survivors.

n: British child migration programmes — IICSA
place: Sent from the UK to Australia, Canada, New Zealand and Southern Rhodesia
who: UK government; Fairbridge Society, Barnardo's, Sisters of Nazareth, Catholic Church agencies and others; receiving institutions incl. Christian Brothers
cover: Successive governments continued the policy despite years of evidence that children were suffering, including sexual abuse. Fairbridge failed to respond properly to a series of sexual abuse allegations at its schools.
d: IICSA's report of 1 March 2018 found that the child migration programmes were 'a deeply flawed government policy' and that successive UK governments failed to ensure protections against abuse. It found a catalogue of evidence that migrated children suffered ill-treatment and abuse including sexual abuse; Barnardo's suspended migration after sexual abuse came to light at its Picton school, and the Fairbridge Society failed to respond to allegations at its schools in Canada and Australia. It recommended an immediate financial redress scheme for surviving child migrants.

n: Round Table on Residential Care (Runder Tisch Heimerziehung) — West German children's homes 1950s–70s
who: State and church-run children's homes in West Germany
d: The Bundestag-appointed Round Table on residential care in the 1950s and 1960s presented its final report in December 2010. It found brutal discipline, humiliation, beatings and forced labour were common, and about one in three of those who contacted it reported sexual abuse. It recommended a fund of at least €120 million to be paid in equal thirds by the federal government, the states and the churches.

n: Wilhelminenberg children's home, Vienna — commission report
who: City of Vienna children's home at Wilhelminenberg
cover: Municipal staff in the overseeing department knew of widespread abuse and did not act; city politicians who learned of it in the 1960s also ignored it.
d: A commission set up by the City of Vienna presented a 344-page report on 12 June 2013, based on 217 interviews including 140 former residents. It found children at the city-run home (1948–1977, girls only from 1962) were rampantly abused, including rape and sexual exploitation by caregivers and outside men, with girls as young as about six. Findings were sent to prosecutors. Some former residents received payments of up to €35,000.

n: Finland — maltreatment in child welfare substitute care 1937–1983
who: Finnish child welfare institutions and foster care
d: A Ministry of Social Affairs and Health study interviewed about 300 people who had been in child welfare substitute care between 1937 and 1983 and found maltreatment and violence in all forms of care. The Finnish government made an official apology on 20 November 2016, Universal Children's Day.

n: Mount Cashel Orphanage, St John's — Hughes Royal Commission
place: Mount Cashel Orphanage, St John's, Newfoundland
who: Mount Cashel Orphanage run by the Irish Christian Brothers, with privileged foster-home status from Newfoundland Social Services; Royal Newfoundland Constabulary; provincial Department of Justice
cover: In December 1975 the police chief and assistant chief ordered Detective Robert Hillier to end his investigation after two Brothers admitted molestation; references to sexual assault were removed and the first report destroyed. The Justice Department laid no charges, and four Brothers were moved out of the province instead.
d: Complaints of abuse at Mount Cashel surfaced in 1974 and 1975 but neither led to charges. Police reopened the case in February 1989; nine Christian Brothers were convicted. The Hughes Royal Commission (156 hearing days, over 200 witnesses, report 31 May 1991) found neither the police nor the Justice Department handled the 1975–76 files normally, and that child welfare director Frank Simms insisted on special treatment for the Brothers. The province paid $11 million to more than 40 victims in 1997.

n: Federal Indian Boarding Schools — Interior Department investigation
place: United States (417 schools in 37 states or territories)
who: US Department of the Interior / federal government; many schools run by churches with federal funding
d: The Federal Indian Boarding School Initiative's Volume I (May 2022) and Volume II (July 2024) identified 417 federal Indian boarding schools in 37 states or then-territories between 1819 and 1969, at least 973 children's deaths, and at least 74 marked and unmarked burial sites at 65 schools. The report states that many Indian children suffered 'physical, sexual, and emotional abuse' at the schools and recommended a formal US apology.

n: US juvenile facilities — BJS National Survey of Youth in Custody 2018
who: State and locally run juvenile detention and correctional facilities
d: The Bureau of Justice Statistics surveyed 6,049 youth in 327 juvenile facilities between March and December 2018. 7.1% reported sexual victimisation in the previous 12 months, and 5.8% reported sexual misconduct by staff (down from 7.7% in 2012). Youth-on-youth forced or coerced victimisation was reported by 1.9%.

n: Illinois state youth detention centres and Cook County JTDC — mass abuse lawsuits
place: Illinois (incl. Illinois Youth Center St. Charles and Cook County Juvenile Temporary Detention Center, Chicago)
who: Illinois Department of Juvenile Justice (nine state youth detention centres, five since closed); Cook County Juvenile Temporary Detention Center
d: Between May and September 2024, 667 former detainees sued alleging sexual abuse by staff at Illinois state youth detention centres and the Cook County Juvenile Temporary Detention Center; three suits filed on 23 September 2024 alone covered 272 plaintiffs and abuse from 1996 to 2021. The lawsuits name repeat alleged abusers, including a chaplain at St. Charles, and say at least one accused employee still worked for the state. These are allegations not yet tested in court.

n: Bringing Them Home — Stolen Generations inquiry
who: Commonwealth, state and territory governments; church and state institutions, foster and adoptive families
cover: The report documented officials misrepresenting capable parents as unfit and telling some parents their children had died when they had not.
d: The Human Rights and Equal Opportunity Commission's 'Bringing Them Home' report on the forced removal of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander children was released on 26 May 1997 with 54 recommendations. Survivors described abuse, including sexual abuse, in institutions and foster care. Recommendation five, a national apology, was refused by the Howard government and delivered by Prime Minister Kevin Rudd in 2008; the recommended national compensation scheme was refused by successive governments. The report recorded rates of sexual assault among its witnesses (record cites 17% of women and 7.7% of men among 502 witnesses; not re-checked from the report itself).

n: Scouting Ireland — 'Historical Sexual Abuse in Scouting: A Learning Review' (Elliott)
place: Ireland (Larch Hill, Co. Dublin national office)
who: Catholic Boy Scouts of Ireland (CBSI) and Scout Association of Ireland (SAI), merged as Scouting Ireland in 2004
cover: The review found 'coverup and a failure to report abuse'; records were lost or destroyed; adults with a sexual interest in young people rose to positions of influence and prevented known offenders being removed.
d: Child-protection consultant Ian Elliott's 'Historical Sexual Abuse in Scouting: A Learning Review', published by Scouting Ireland on 14 May 2020, found a cover-up and failure to report abuse in the former Catholic Boy Scouts of Ireland and Scout Association of Ireland. It described 'a culture driven by self-interest', said 'cronyism thrived', and found that people suspected or known to be sex offenders gained positions of power and became 'largely impregnable'; records had been lost or destroyed, so the full extent could not be determined. An earlier audit reported to the Oireachtas in November 2018 had found evidence of 108 alleged victims and 71 alleged abusers, with numbers expected to rise considerably.

n: TISS 'Koshish' social audit of 110 Bihar children's homes
place: Bihar (38 districts; incl. Muzaffarpur, Motihari, Bhagalpur, Munger)
who: Children's and girls' homes funded by the Bihar Social Welfare Department, many NGO-run
cover: In the audited Bhagalpur home staff refused to give the audit team the key to the complaint box, saying it was lost; the department's director evaded questions about action on the other 14 homes.
d: At the Bihar government's request, the Koshish unit of the Tata Institute of Social Sciences visited 110 children's homes in 38 districts and submitted its audit to the Social Welfare Department on 27 April 2018, grading homes as better, administrative negligence or criminal negligence. The Muzaffarpur girls' home run by Sewa Sankalp Evam Vikas Samiti was graded criminal negligence, and the report raised harassment or abuse at 14 other homes, including a girls' home with complaints of severe sexual harassment and violence and homes where children were routinely beaten. The audit triggered the Muzaffarpur FIR of 31 May 2018 and later CBI cases against other Bihar shelter homes.

n: Casitas del Sur — children missing from church-run shelters
place: Mexico City (also CAIFAC, Monterrey; 'La Casita', Cancún)
who: Iglesia Cristiana Restaurada (Restored Christian Church) shelters; Mexico City Attorney General's Office (PGJDF), which placed children there
cover: A Mexico City legislator accused officials of the District Attorney's office of negligence and complicity, saying they warned the shelter of searches so children could be moved.
d: Children placed by Mexico City prosecutors in the private Casitas del Sur shelter, run by a church group, went missing. In October 2010 Mexico's federal Attorney General offered rewards for information on 14 children who disappeared in February 2009 from the Casitas del Sur shelter in Mexico City and from related homes in Nuevo Laredo and Quintana Roo, and about 5 million pesos for three people sought in the case, saying the children may have been taken by child traffickers. Earlier sources not re-checked for this map also cite the removal of 126 children by police and human rights staff on 29 January 2009 and obstruction charges against seven staff (not re-checked for this map).

n: Provo Canyon School, Utah — licences revoked 2026
who: Provo Canyon School, owned by Universal Health Services (2000–2026)
d: Provo Canyon School opened in 1971 and has faced abuse allegations for more than 50 years; former students including Paris Hilton (who attended in the 1990s under different ownership) have publicly described abuse. In 2026, after a 13-year-old boy was seriously injured in a fight and staff did not call 911 or seek immediate care, Utah's Department of Health and Human Services revoked the licence of the school's Springville campus and, on 17 July 2026, of its original Provo campus, citing failure to protect children from harm and abuse, 'cruel and unnecessary' pain-compliance techniques, prolonged restraints and humiliating discipline. Owner Universal Health Services (since 2000) said it disagreed and was reviewing appeal options. No official sexual-abuse finding was located; the licence revocations concerned abuse, mistreatment and safety.

n: The Scout Association (UK) — abuse claims and payouts
who: The Scout Association (UK)
d: A BBC File on 4 investigation in June 2023 found, from data from eight specialist law firms, that at least 260 child sexual abuse claims had been taken on against the Scouts in the previous decade and more than £6m paid out across 166 settled cases. The Scouts said 96% of claims highlighted by a survivors' campaign related to offences before 2013 and that the payouts broadly matched what it knew. In 2014 the BBC had reported more than 50 historical claims and £897,000 in damages; an MP called for an inquiry into failures to pass abuse records to police.

n: Ukraine orphanages as a 'recruitment tool' for traffickers — Disability Rights International 'No Way Home'
place: Ukraine (33 institutions visited, incl. Vinnytsia oblast)
who: Ukrainian state orphanages, boarding schools and institutions for children with disabilities
d: Disability Rights International investigated 33 institutions between 2012 and 2015 and published 'No Way Home' in 2015. La Strada Ukraine told DRI that recruiting children from orphanages into prostitution is 'the most typical scheme' and that sexual exploitation in institutions typically begins around age 13, often instigated by staff; an IOM counter-trafficking coordinator called orphanages a direct feeder to domestic and international trafficking and said most documented cases originate in the vocational schools that orphanage leavers attend. DRI concluded that the orphanage system serves as a recruitment tool for traffickers.

n: Deoria shelter home, Uttar Pradesh — girls rescued, CBI case
who: Maa Vindhyavasini Mahila Prashikshan Evam Samaj Sewa Sansthan (NGO); director Girija Tripathi and superintendent Kanchan Lata Tripathi
cover: The UP Women and Child Development Minister said the NGO's recognition had been revoked and funds stopped a year earlier, yet it continued to operate; the government said it would examine who was responsible.
d: The case came to light when a 10-year-old girl escaped to a women's police station and said girls were taken away in cars in the afternoons and returned crying in the morning. Police rescued 24 girls on 5 August 2018 and sealed the home. Police charge-sheeted the director and her daughter, and seven others in a second FIR. In 2019 the CBI took over and registered cases including sexual harassment, human trafficking, sexual assault and adoption without legal procedure.

n: Seth Sevana children's home, Vavuniya — monk arrested, bail with NCPA consent
who: Seth Sevana Lama Nivasa children's home (run by a Buddhist monk) housing war-affected Tamil children; National Child Protection Authority (NCPA)
cover: Complaints had been made to the NCPA since 2010; the arrest came only after protests by Vavuniya child protection officers. On 31 December 2013 the monk got unconditional bail after the Attorney General's Department, on NCPA instructions, told the court it had no objection; the NCPA did not submit the 22 children's reports to the court.
d: In October 2013 the head of a children's home in Vavuniya, a Buddhist monk, was arrested for sexually abusing a 9-year-old child, confirmed by medical evidence on 12 October 2013. The NCPA took custody of the other 22 children on 15 October 2013. Most children were war-affected Tamil children placed by poor families. Groundviews reported that complaints had reached the NCPA since 2010 and that the agency later supported his release on bail.

n: Uganda — over 500 unlicensed children's homes outside state oversight
place: Uganda (Kampala, Wakiso, Mukono, Jinja and other districts)
who: Uganda Ministry of Gender, Labour and Social Development; unlicensed children's homes, many foreign-funded
d: Uganda's Ministry of Gender, Labour and Social Development says only 185 children's homes are fully licensed (holding 9,486 children) and that more than 500 unlicensed institutions operate without oversight, exposing children to neglect, exploitation and abuse. The ministry's principal probation officer said many children in homes are not orphans, and that some are survivors of trafficking or sexual abuse. The government has closed unregistered homes, including Hope Center Uganda (American board) after a raid that found children in poor conditions.

n: MONUC peacekeepers — sexual exploitation of girls in Bunia (OIOS 2004)
who: UN Organization Mission in the DRC (MONUC) military contingents, military observers and civilian staff
d: After media and Congolese women's reports in March and May 2004, OIOS investigated in Bunia from May to September 2004. It found that sexual contact with peacekeepers occurred 'with regularity', usually in exchange for food or small sums of money, and that many cases involved girls under 18, some as young as 13. Of 72 allegations reported to MONUC, many could not be investigated because they were non-specific; six cases were fully substantiated. The findings led to the Secretary-General asking Prince Zeid Ra'ad Al-Hussein of Jordan to prepare the 2005 comprehensive report on SEA by peacekeepers.

n: MINUSCA peacekeepers — rapes near Bambari airport
who: MINUSCA contingents believed by survivors to be from the Republic of Congo or DR Congo
d: Human Rights Watch documented eight cases of sexual exploitation and abuse by MINUSCA peacekeepers during research in Bambari in January 2016, including a 14-year-old girl and an 18-year-old woman who said they were gang-raped near Bambari airport. Most incidents occurred between September and December 2015, when a Republic of Congo contingent guarded the airport.

n: Kosovo — trafficking for forced prostitution and the international presence (Amnesty 2004)
who: Criminal networks; demand from NATO KFOR soldiers, UN police and international staff
cover: Amnesty found no evidence of criminal proceedings against any military personnel in their home countries.
d: Amnesty International's May 2004 report said Kosovo had become a major destination for women and girls trafficked for forced prostitution since NATO troops and UN administrators arrived in 1999, with the international presence generating 80% of traffickers' income at the time. Women and girls were brought mainly from Moldova, Romania, Ukraine and Russia via Serbia, and local girls were also abducted. The UN peacekeeping department acknowledged in 2004 that peacekeepers had 'come to be seen as part of the problem in trafficking rather than the solution'.

n: Ebola response, North Kivu & Ituri — Independent Commission on SEA by WHO and other responders
place: Beni, Butembo, Mangina (North Kivu) and Ituri
who: WHO staff and contractors, Ministry of Health and partner personnel in the 10th Ebola response
d: The Independent Commission appointed by WHO reported on 28 September 2021 that it identified 83 alleged perpetrators, 21 of whom were established with certainty as WHO employees during the response; most were Congolese staff hired temporarily who used their authority to obtain sex, often in exchange for jobs. The review team heard 63 women and 12 men aged 13 to 43; the youngest, a girl selling phone cards in Mangina in April 2019, said a WHO driver raped her. Nine rape allegations were recorded and 29 women and girls became pregnant.

n: Sudan — RSF rape and sexual slavery of women and girls (UN Fact-Finding Mission 2024)
place: Darfur (El Geneina, West Darfur) and Khartoum
who: Rapid Support Forces and allied militias; also some cases by Sudanese Armed Forces
d: The independent international fact-finding mission for the Sudan found that rape and gang rape were widespread, mostly by men in RSF uniform and allied militias, with victims including girls as young as 8. It found the abduction and detention of women and girls for sexual purposes by the RSF amounted to sexual slavery. The UN Secretary-General verified sexual violence against 114 girls in 2023 (RSF 57) and 74 children in 2024 (RSF 54, RSF-affiliated militia 9) and listed the RSF for rape and abduction of children.

n: Bosnia — Foča rape camps; ICTY Kunarac judgment (girls as young as 12 enslaved)
who: Bosnian Serb army (VRS) and paramilitaries; local police chief named in testimony
d: In Serb-held Foča in 1992–93, Bosniak women and girls were held at detention sites such as Partizan Sports Hall, next to the municipal police building, and taken from there to apartments and private houses to be raped; the ICTY found rape was used by Bosnian Serb forces as an instrument of terror and that local police guarded the women and joined in their mistreatment. On 22 February 2001 the ICTY sentenced Dragoljub Kunarac, a VRS reconnaissance unit leader, to 28 years for torture, rape and enslavement; Radomir Kovač to 20 years for enslavement, rape and outrages upon personal dignity, including detaining two girls in his apartment for about four months and selling victims to other soldiers; and Zoran Vuković to 12 years for torture and rape, including raping a girl he knew to be 15. The sentences were upheld on appeal on 12 June 2002.

n: Dapchi schoolgirls abduction — ISWAP/Boko Haram
place: Government Girls Science and Technical College, Dapchi, Yobe
who: Boko Haram faction (ISWAP)
d: On the evening of 19 February 2018 militants stormed Dapchi, Yobe state, and abducted girls from a boarding school; Nigeria's government said 110 schoolgirls were missing. On 21 March 2018 the government said 106 children — 104 schoolgirls, a girl who did not attend the school and a boy — had been freed, and denied paying a ransom. Five girls were reported to have died during the journey after the abduction. The only Christian girl in the group, who refused to convert, remained in captivity.

n: LRA Makombo massacre and abductions, DR Congo (2009)
who: Lord's Resistance Army commanders Lt. Col. Binansio Okumu ('Binany') and 'Obol', reporting to Gen. Dominic Ongwen (per HRW)
d: From 14 to 17 December 2009 Lord's Resistance Army forces attacked at least 10 villages in the remote Makombo area of Haute-Uélé, north-eastern DR Congo, killing at least 321 civilians and abducting 250 others, including at least 80 children. Human Rights Watch, which documented the previously unreported massacre after a field mission in February 2010, said it was carried out by two LRA commanders who reported to Gen. Dominic Ongwen, the senior LRA leader believed to command its forces in Congo and wanted by the International Criminal Court.

n: Mozambique, Cabo Delgado — abduction of children by ISIS-linked armed groups
place: Cabo Delgado province (Macomia, Mocímboa da Praia, Muidumbe)
who: Islamic State–Mozambique Province ('Al-Shabaab' locally) and other armed groups; also Mozambique defence forces (sexual violence, 2023)
d: The UN verified the abduction of 468 children (371 boys, 97 girls) by armed groups in Cabo Delgado in 2024, 392 for recruitment, and sexual violence against 5 girls. In 2023 it verified 92 abductions (4 for sexual violence) and sexual violence against 12 girls attributed to the Mozambique Defence Armed Forces (5), armed groups (4) and the police Rapid Intervention Unit (3).

n: Mali — UN-verified rape and abduction of children (2022–2024)
who: JNIM, ISGS, Malian armed forces, foreign security personnel and others
d: The UN verified the rape of 32 girls in Mali in 2024 by unidentified perpetrators (22), ISGS (4), JNIM (3), the Malian armed forces (2) and Ganda Lassal Izo (1), and the abduction of 119 children, including 4 by foreign security personnel. In 2023 it verified the rape of 15 girls, 4 by the Malian armed forces.

n: Yemen — sexual violence against children by government-affiliated forces and Houthis (UN verified)
who: Yemen Armed Forces and affiliated forces (police, Security Belt, Amaliqah); Houthis
d: The UN verified sexual violence against 24 children (8 boys, 16 girls) in Yemen in 2023, 20 attributed to the Yemen Armed Forces and affiliated forces (Yemen Armed Forces 9, Yemeni police 4). In 2024 it verified 11 cases (6 boys, 5 girls), attributed to the Houthis (2), Yemen Armed Forces (2) and affiliated forces (7), including Yemeni police (4).

n: Syria — abduction of children by armed groups and government forces (UN verified)
who: Patriotic Revolutionary Youth Movement, Syrian government forces, YPG/YPJ
d: The UN verified the abduction of 14 children (5 boys, 9 girls) in Syria in 2024 by the Patriotic Revolutionary Youth Movement (9), Syrian government forces (4) and YPG/YPJ (1), often for recruitment and use.

n: Bosco Ntaganda (UPC/FPLC, Ituri) — ICC conviction incl. rape and sexual slavery of child soldiers
who: Union of Congolese Patriots (UPC) / Patriotic Forces for the Liberation of Congo (FPLC)
d: On 8 July 2019 ICC Trial Chamber VI found Bosco Ntaganda guilty of 18 counts of war crimes and crimes against humanity committed in Ituri in 2002–2003, including rape, sexual slavery and the conscription and use of children under 15; he was the first person convicted of sexual slavery by the ICC. He was sentenced to 30 years on 7 November 2019, confirmed on appeal on 30 March 2021. He had told child soldiers, 'When you're a soldier, you get a woman for free'.

n: Chad — sexual violence against girls by the Chadian National Army (UN verified 2022)
place: Lac Province (Lake Chad basin) and Sudan border areas
who: Chadian National Army
d: The UN verified rape and other sexual violence against three girls by the Chadian National Army in Lac Province in 2022, and in Sudan attributed 4 of 35 cases of sexual violence against girls aged 12 to 17 to the Chadian National Army. In the Lake Chad basin it verified the abduction of 191 children in Lac Province and Diffa.

n: Epstein — 2019 federal sex-trafficking indictment and death in custody
who: Jeffrey Epstein; Metropolitan Correctional Center (Bureau of Prisons)
cover: DOJ Inspector General (June 2023) found negligence and misconduct by Bureau of Prisons staff: 13 employees showed misconduct, two were criminally charged, guards skipped required checks and falsified records, and Epstein was left without a cellmate after an apparent July 23 suicide attempt.
d: Epstein was arrested at Teterboro Airport on 6 July 2019 and indicted in Manhattan for sex trafficking of minors in 2002–2005. Bail was denied on 18 July. He died in his cell on 10 August 2019; the medical examiner ruled suicide by hanging and the case was dismissed on 29 August 2019. The DOJ Inspector General's June 2023 report found no evidence contradicting suicide but documented staff failures that made it possible.

n: Zorro Ranch, New Mexico — state probe dropped in 2019, reopened 2026
place: Near Stanley, Santa Fe County, New Mexico
who: Jeffrey Epstein; New Mexico law enforcement
cover: The state AG's 2019 investigation was closed at the request of the US Attorney's Office (SDNY). The 2026 interim commission report found Epstein likely got 'preferential treatment' from New Mexico law enforcement, avoided sex-offender registration via a loophole, and used NDAs, secrecy protocols and a $7m-a-year payroll to keep activity out of view. The FBI never searched the ranch in 2019.
d: Epstein bought the 7,600-acre ranch in 1993. New Mexico AG Raúl Torrez reopened a criminal investigation on 12 March 2026 citing previously sealed FBI files, and state officials searched the ranch in March 2026 with the new owners' cooperation. A four-member legislative truth commission created in the 2026 session released a 119-page interim report on 5 Aug 2026; a final report is due by end of 2026. Allegations that bodies were buried near the ranch, raised in the files, are unconfirmed.

n: Ankara prosecutors' inquiry into alleged trafficking of girls from Turkey to Epstein
who: Ankara Chief Public Prosecutor's Office (inquiry)
d: On 23 Dec 2025 Ankara prosecutors reportedly opened an inquiry after opposition MP Turhan Çömez cited the DOJ files. The underlying document is a May 2009 civil complaint by 'Jane Doe No. 102' alleging 'upon information and belief' that Epstein brought minor girls from 'Turkey, the Czech Republic, Asia, and numerous other countries'. Prosecutors are reviewing the files; no findings or charges have been reported.

n: Dame Janet Smith Review — Savile and Stuart Hall at the BBC
who: BBC
cover: Some BBC staff knew of complaints about Savile and Hall but did not pass them to senior management; Hall's celebrity status discouraged staff from escalating.
d: The independent review by Dame Janet Smith, published on 25 February 2016, found that Savile sexually abused 72 people in connection with his BBC work, raping eight, the youngest victim aged eight; incidents dated back to 1959. It found that Stuart Hall assaulted 21 girls and women in connection with the BBC between 1967 and 1991, the youngest aged 10. Some staff knew of complaints, but a 'culture of fear' and deference to stars meant these were not passed to senior managers; two senior managers were 'aware' or 'probably aware' of Hall's assaults on BBC premises.

n: Operation Midland — Carl Beech's false 'VIP ring' claims
who: Metropolitan Police; Carl Beech (complainant)
d: Between November 2014 and March 2016 the Met investigated Carl Beech's claims that a VIP ring of politicians and military and security chiefs abused boys and committed murders, including at Dolphin Square. It searched homes of named suspects, including Leon Brittan, Harvey Proctor and Lord Bramall, but arrested and charged no one. Sir Richard Henriques's review (Nov 2016) found police had been taken in by false allegations and listed 43 failings. In July 2019 Beech was jailed for 18 years for 12 counts of perverting the course of justice and one of fraud, and for child sexual offences he had admitted, including possessing indecent images of children and covertly filming a teenage boy.

n: Barry Bennell and English youth football (Sheldon Review)
who: Barry Bennell (coach/scout, Crewe Alexandra, Manchester City links); The Football Association
cover: Crewe Alexandra heard an allegation but kept Bennell on with restrictions (former director Hamilton Smith). The Sheldon Review found the FA guilty of 'institutional failure' for delaying safeguards after 1995.
d: Bennell was first jailed in Florida in 1994 for raping a British boy on a football tour, then received prison sentences in Britain in 1998, 2015, February 2018 (50 offences against 12 boys aged eight to 14, 1979–1990; 30 years) and October 2020 (a fifth sentence, making 34 years in total). After a former player spoke out publicly in November 2016, BBC News reported within weeks that 350 people had alleged they were victims, linked to 55 clubs. Clive Sheldon QC's review for the FA (17 Mar 2021) recorded at least 240 suspects and 692 survivors across football, said the true numbers were likely far higher, found the FA had acted 'far too slowly' on child protection, and criticised Manchester City, Crewe and Stoke over Bennell. Bennell died in prison in September 2023.

n: Casa Pia — abuse of children in state care by a TV presenter, diplomat and others
who: Casa Pia (state children's institution); Carlos Cruz (TV presenter); Jorge Ritto (ex-ambassador); Hugo Marçal (lawyer); Ferreira Diniz (doctor); Manuel Abrantes (Casa Pia official); Carlos Silvino (driver)
cover: A teacher reportedly began reporting abuse to Casa Pia leaders and police in 1975, and police accused a caretaker in 1981, without legal action. Ritto had been removed as consul in Stuttgart around 1969–71 after a complaint about an under-age boy, but stayed in the diplomatic service.
d: Abuse at Casa Pia, a state institution caring for about 4,500 children, is said to have begun in the mid-1970s and came to light in 2002. After a trial that began in 2004, on 3 Sept 2010 six of seven defendants were convicted: former Casa Pia driver Carlos Silvino (18 years, after confessing to 639 charges of abusing boys or procuring them for others), TV presenter Carlos Cruz (7), doctor João Ferreira Diniz (7), retired ambassador Jorge Ritto (6y8m), lawyer Hugo Marçal (6y2m) and former Casa Pia governor Manuel Abrantes (5y9m); a woman accused of letting her house be used was acquitted. The convicted men other than Silvino denied the charges. Former minister Paulo Pedroso was detained during the investigation but was not tried.

n: Lord Greville Janner — allegations from Leicestershire children's homes; never tried
who: Greville Janner (Labour MP and peer); Leicestershire Police; Crown Prosecution Service
cover: Police investigated in 1991, 2002 and 2007 without charges. The Henriques report (Jan 2016) found the CPS and police at fault and said a prosecution was likely to have succeeded in 1991, 2002 or 2007. A 2021 review found police 'appeared reluctant to fully investigate'.
d: Allegations that Janner abused boys in Leicestershire children's homes first emerged publicly in 1991. In April 2015 the CPS decided not to charge him because of dementia; an independent review reversed this in June 2015, but he was found unfit to stand trial in Dec 2015 and died on 19 Dec 2015 before a 'trial of the facts'. He was never convicted. A January 2016 report by retired judge Sir Richard Henriques found that the CPS and Leicestershire Police had mishandled investigations in 1991, 2002 and 2007 and that there had been enough evidence to prosecute him in 2007.

n: Spiniak case, Chile — child exploitation ring and false accusation against a senator
who: Claudio Spiniak (businessman)
d: Businessman Claudio Spiniak was arrested in 2003 accused of leading a network that sexually abused and exploited adolescents. In 2008 Chile's Supreme Court sentenced him to 12 years for sexual abuse of minors, promoting their exploitation and producing pornographic material; he was released in 2013 and died in March 2026. A witness claimed that members of Congress attended his parties — claims publicly backed by a deputy and a former priest — but she later admitted she had lied; the politicians named were cleared (proceedings dismissed for lack of evidence). The political-network claim is disproved.

n: Joel Greenberg conviction and House Ethics findings on Matt Gaetz
who: Joel Greenberg (Seminole County tax collector); Rep. Matt Gaetz (not charged)
d: Greenberg pleaded guilty in May 2021 to six federal crimes, including sex trafficking of a minor (a 17-year-old girl in 2017), identity theft, stalking, wire fraud and conspiracy to bribe a public official, and was sentenced to 11 years on 1 Dec 2022. DOJ investigated Rep. Gaetz over whether he paid the same 17-year-old for sex but did not charge him. The House Ethics Committee report (23 Dec 2024) said it received testimony that Gaetz twice had sex with the 17-year-old at a 2017 party and paid her, and found that this violated Florida law, but found insufficient evidence that he violated the federal sex-trafficking statute. Gaetz denies having sex with a minor and has not been charged.

n: Franklin credit union 'child prostitution ring' allegations, Nebraska
who: Claims against Lawrence E. King Jr. (Franklin Community Federal Credit Union) and prominent Nebraskans
d: After the Franklin Community Federal Credit Union in Omaha failed in late 1988 and its manager Lawrence King was accused of embezzling millions, rumours spread that its money had paid for the sexual abuse of minors by prominent Nebraskans. In July 1990 a Douglas County grand jury called the claims a 'carefully crafted hoax' and indicted two people for perjury; a federal grand jury in September 1990 also found the allegations unfounded. King called the sexual allegations 'garbage'. A later civil default judgment against King, who did not respond, is not a finding of fact.

n: Unnao rape case — MLA Kuldeep Singh Sengar
who: Kuldeep Singh Sengar (BJP MLA, Uttar Pradesh)
cover: The victim's father died in police custody; in July 2019 a truck crash killed two of her aunts and critically injured her and her lawyer (a court later accepted the CBI finding of no foul play in the crash). The arrest came only after the Allahabad High Court ordered it in 2018.
d: Sengar, then a BJP MLA in Uttar Pradesh, was convicted in December 2019 by a special CBI court in Delhi of raping a minor girl in Unnao district in 2017, and sentenced to life imprisonment; the BJP had expelled him. In December 2025 the Delhi High Court suspended his sentence; on 29 Dec 2025 the Supreme Court stayed that order on the CBI's appeal, and in May 2026 it set the suspension aside, directing the High Court to decide his appeal against conviction within three months or pass a fresh order.

n: Brisbane Grammar / St Paul's — counsellor abuse; Governor-General resigns over church handling
who: Brisbane Grammar School; St Paul's School; Anglican Diocese of Brisbane (Archbishop Peter Hollingworth)
cover: Brisbane Grammar quietly investigated complaints about counsellor Kevin Lynch in the early 1980s; he moved to St Paul's. A 2003 diocesan inquiry found Archbishop Hollingworth in 1993 allowed a known abuser to keep working as a priest.
d: School counsellor Kevin John Lynch, who worked at Brisbane Grammar and then at the Anglican St Paul's School in the 1980s and 1990s, abused students; music teacher Gregory Knight at St Paul's was a convicted paedophile. Peter Hollingworth was Anglican Archbishop of Brisbane from 1989 to 2001. An Anglican church inquiry report, tabled in the Queensland parliament on 1 May 2003, found he had acted unfairly in some cases, notably in allowing a known paedophile to continue as a priest; he resigned as Governor-General on 25 May 2003. In November 2015 the Royal Commission into Institutional Responses to Child Sexual Abuse examined the two schools' handling of the abuse, and Hollingworth apologised to victims.

n: Westchester County grand jury — Archdiocese of New York (2002)
place: White Plains, Westchester County, New York
who: Catholic Archdiocese of New York
cover: Grand jury called the church's handling of complaints 'an orchestrated effort to protect abusing clergy members from investigation, arrest and prosecution'
d: A Westchester County grand jury issued a 13-page report in June 2002 after a two-month inquiry that reviewed tens of thousands of pages of archdiocesan documents and heard from eight alleged victims. It found the church's handling of abuse claims was an orchestrated effort to shield abusing clergy from investigation and prosecution. It recommended making it a felony for church officials not to report allegations and ending the statute of limitations for crimes against minors. The archdiocese called the report unfair.

n: Philadelphia grand jury — Archdiocese of Philadelphia (2005)
who: Catholic Archdiocese of Philadelphia
cover: Grand jury found Cardinals John Krol and Anthony Bevilacqua knew of the abuse and covered it up; the archdiocese disputes this
d: A Philadelphia grand jury released a 418-page report in September 2005 finding that at least 63 priests of the archdiocese had abused hundreds of minors over several decades. It found that Cardinals John Krol and Anthony Bevilacqua knew of the abuse and concealed it. No charges were brought because most cases fell outside the time limit for prosecution.

n: Florida Office of Statewide Prosecution — Catholic clergy abuse (2020)
who: Catholic dioceses of Florida
cover: Florida was a state where accused priests were 'routinely relocated'; the report found acts by the church that enabled sexual abuse of minors
d: Florida's Office of Statewide Prosecution closed a two-year investigation, opened after the 2018 Pennsylvania grand jury report, with a report released on 6 November 2020. It found historical sexual abuse allegations against 97 priests in Florida, none of whom could be prosecuted because of the statute of limitations, earlier prosecution or death. It found that accused priests had been routinely relocated and that church acts had enabled abuse of minors, but found no evidence of ongoing unreported abuse. More than 260 tips were received.

n: Kansas Bureau of Investigation — Catholic clergy abuse (2023)
who: Catholic Archdiocese of Kansas City in Kansas and other Kansas dioceses
cover: The KBI found the church protected suspected clergy for decades, often by transferring priests to other churches; some victims were bound by non-disclosure agreements
d: A four-year Kansas Bureau of Investigation inquiry, requested by Archbishop Joseph Naumann and reported in January 2023, reviewed five decades of church records and identified 188 clergy suspected of crimes such as rape and sexual misconduct with children. Investigators spoke with nearly 140 victims, witnesses and suspects in 15 states and referred 30 cases to prosecutors, all of which were too old to charge. The KBI found the church had protected these men for decades, often by moving them to other parishes.

n: Prosecuting Attorneys' Council of Georgia — Atlanta and Savannah (2023)
who: Catholic Archdiocese of Atlanta; Diocese of Savannah
cover: Some accused priests were reassigned without notice to officials at their new posts; historical church policies 'enabled sexual abuse of minors'
d: A review by the Prosecuting Attorneys' Council of Georgia, dated 20 March 2023 and covering both dioceses that together span the whole state, found credible allegations of child sexual abuse against 28 priests while serving in Georgia, dating back to the 1940s. It found that some accused priests were reassigned without notice and that historical policies enabled abuse; Savannah began taking allegations seriously in the late 1980s and Atlanta in the 1990s. No case could be prosecuted.

n: US Senate inquiry — Olympic movement and the FBI failed to protect athletes (2019)
who: US Olympic Committee; USA Gymnastics; FBI; Michigan State University
cover: The report found the USOC, USA Gymnastics and other governing bodies took actions to conceal their negligence, and that the USOC and the FBI 'fundamentally failed' to protect gymnasts
d: An 18-month investigation by the Senate Commerce subcommittee led by Senators Jerry Moran and Richard Blumenthal reported on 30 July 2019. It found that the US Olympic Committee and the FBI 'fundamentally failed' to protect gymnasts from Larry Nassar, and that the USOC, USA Gymnastics and other governing bodies took actions to conceal their negligence. It found institutions repeatedly failed to report wrongdoing to law enforcement. The senators proposed the Empowering Olympic and Amateur Athletes Act to reform oversight of Olympic sport.

n: GAO-11-200 — US schools hired or kept staff with histories of sexual misconduct (2010)
who: Public and private K-12 schools in 11 US states
cover: School officials let teachers resign rather than face discipline and in some cases gave positive references that helped them get jobs at other schools; some schools did no criminal history check
d: The US Government Accountability Office released GAO-11-200 on 16 December 2010 after examining 15 cases in 11 states where schools hired or retained people with histories of sexual misconduct. In at least 11 cases the offenders had previously targeted children and in at least 6 they abused more children after being hired. Officials sometimes allowed resignations instead of discipline and wrote positive references; some schools did no fingerprint-based checks. GAO found no federal law governing the employment of sex offenders in schools.

n: Law Commission of Canada — 'Restoring Dignity': child abuse in Canadian institutions (2000)
who: Government-run and government-funded institutions for children, including Indian residential schools
d: In November 1997 the federal Minister of Justice asked the Law Commission of Canada to report on processes for dealing with physical and sexual abuse of children in government-run, government-funded and government-sponsored institutions. Its report, Restoring Dignity: Responding to Child Abuse in Canadian Institutions, was presented in March 2000. It reviewed the history of residential schools and other institutions and assessed redress options, recommending programmes negotiated with survivors that avoid causing further harm, together with public education and prevention measures.

n: Victoria — 'Betrayal of Trust' parliamentary inquiry into religious and other organisations (2013)
who: Catholic Church and other religious and non-government organisations in Victoria
cover: The inquiry found the Catholic Church's early-1990s response continued to conceal abuse; senior church representatives conceded steps intended to conceal wrongdoing
d: The Family and Community Development Committee of the Parliament of Victoria tabled 'Betrayal of Trust', its report of the Inquiry into the Handling of Child Abuse by Religious and Other Non-Government Organisations, in November 2013. It found 'substantial criminal child abuse' over a long period by priests and members of religious orders in Victoria, and a culture in religious organisations that allowed systemic criminal abuse. Its recommendations would compel religious leaders to report child abuse to police and strip the Catholic Church of its virtual immunity from being sued.

n: South Australia — Child Protection Systems Royal Commission, 'The Life They Deserve' (2016)
who: Families SA (state child protection agency); carer Shannon McCoole
cover: The inquiry examined how Families SA failed to prevent abuse by a carer it employed
d: Former Supreme Court Justice Margaret Nyland led a two-year royal commission into South Australia's child protection system, set up in 2014 after Families SA carer Shannon McCoole was charged with sexual offences against children in his care; McCoole was later jailed for 35 years. Her report, 'The Life They Deserve', was delivered to the Governor on 5 August 2016 with 260 recommendations. It found that many children in state care had been abused and neglected not only by their families but also let down by the system meant to protect them.

n: Poland — State Commission on Paedophilia, first and second reports (2021–2022)
who: Polish justice system; Catholic clergy (almost 30% of perpetrators in the cases studied)
d: Poland's State Commission on Paedophilia, set up by the government after a 2020 documentary on abuse and alleged cover-ups in the Catholic Church, published its first report on 29 July 2021. It analysed 345 cases and 245 court proceedings involving 188 girls and 173 boys, most aged 11 to 15. Almost 30% of perpetrators were clergy and 35% were relatives. In half the cases no one had noticed signs of abuse. The commission sent 137 notifications to prosecutors and made 22 recommendations, including ending the statute of limitations for child sexual abuse. Its second report, published on 2 August 2022, covered 513 cases; among abusers who were not relatives, clergy were the largest professional group (57 cases, about 47%).

n: France — CIIVISE final report on sexual violence against children (2023)
who: French justice, health and child-protection systems; families and institutions
d: The Independent Commission on Incest and Sexual Violence against Children (CIIVISE), created by the government on 11 March 2021 and chaired by juvenile judge Édouard Durand, delivered its final report on 20 November 2023 with 82 recommendations. It estimated that 160,000 children suffer sexual violence each year in France. It found that victims wait 10 to 13 years on average for specialised care and that only 5% of reports come from doctors. The commission's work covers abuse in families and in institutions, and the failures of courts, police and health services to act.

n: Germany — Conference of Religious Superiors (DOK) survey of abuse in Catholic orders (2020)
who: Catholic religious orders in Germany (100 of 291 responding orders)
d: The German Conference of Catholic Religious Superiors (DOK) surveyed 392 orders and published the results on 26 August 2020. The 291 orders that answered, covering 88% of members, recorded accusations against at least 654 members and 58 other staff, from at least 1,412 children, adolescents or wards, about 80% of them male. Accusations were recorded in 53 of 77 male orders and 47 of 214 female orders. About 80% of the accused had died. The DOK said there were further unreported cases and that its survey was not a scientific study comparable to the bishops' 2018 study.

n: Germany — SOS-Kinderdorf independent commission report (2024)
who: SOS-Kinderdorf e.V. (Germany) — children's villages and group homes
d: An independent commission appointed by SOS-Kinderdorf e.V. investigated from 2021 and presented its report in Munich on 2 October 2024. It recorded 226 known cases of boundary violations since the organisation's founding in 1955, 189 from its internal reporting office and 37 from a 2023 newspaper appeal, including sexual assaults and in some cases rape. About half were committed by staff such as house parents and about 20% by other young people in care. The commission said the closed nature of SOS family units was a risk and that more cases are likely unrecorded.

n: Germany — Catholic scouts (DPSG) study on sexualised and spiritual violence (2026)
who: Deutsche Pfadfinder*innenschaft Sankt Georg (DPSG), Catholic scout association
d: Researchers from the universities of Marburg and Gießen, led by Sabine Maschke and Ludwig Stecher, studied sexualised and spiritual violence in the Catholic scout association DPSG from 1929 to 2022 and presented the results in Cologne on 5 February 2026. They found sexualised violence was a widespread structural problem, especially on camps and trips, mostly by male leaders against underage girls, and that the association had looked away and played incidents down. Over 90% of the accused were male. The DPSG accepted institutional responsibility.

n: Germany — Diocese of Mainz, EVV study (2023)
who: Catholic Diocese of Mainz
cover: The study faulted Cardinal Karl Lehmann's early years (1983–2001) as 'deflecting and dissembling' and also criticised Bishop Albert Stohr and Cardinal Hermann Volk; Bishop Peter Kohlgraf said that for his predecessors protecting perpetrators and the Church mattered more than those affected.
d: The study 'Erfahren. Verstehen. Vorsorgen.' by lawyer Ulrich Weber, commissioned by the diocese, was released on 3 March 2023. It identified 657 possible victims and 392 suspects for 1945 to 2019, of whom 401 victims and 181 accused remained after review. Weber said Cardinal Karl Lehmann, bishop from 1983 to 2016, never met his own public standard for handling abuse. Bishop Peter Kohlgraf acknowledged major misconduct and omissions under Lehmann, Cardinal Hermann Volk and earlier leaders.

n: Germany — Diocese of Trier independent commission (2022 onward)
who: Catholic Diocese of Trier
cover: Bishop Bernhard Stein (1967–1980) is accused of covering up cases; the commission said it would also examine the terms of Reinhard Marx (bishop 2002–2008) and Georg Bätzing (vicar general 2012–2016).
d: The diocese's independent commission, launched in June 2021 with Gerhard Robbers as spokesman, released its interim report in August 2022 covering 1946 to 2021. It had identified 513 victims and 195 perpetrators so far. University of Trier historians working for the inquiry later published interim reports on abuse during the terms of bishops Bernhard Stein (2022) and Hermann Josef Spital (2024).

n: Belgium (Flanders) — expert panel and Ethiopia investigation on intercountry adoption malpractice
who: Flemish adoption services; intermediaries in Ethiopia and other countries of origin
d: After reports of malpractice in adoptions from Ethiopia in 2019, the Flemish government appointed an independent expert panel on intercountry adoption, which delivered its findings in 2021 (final report dated 15 February 2023), and funded the Flemish Centre for Adoption to examine Ethiopian adoptions from 1997 to 2015. Preliminary conclusions found that the true story sometimes differed from the adoption files and that in the worst cases children had not been given up voluntarily by their birth parents. The panel's report led to screening of every country of origin, after which Flanders stopped adoptions from Vietnam and then from Gambia, Haiti and Morocco.

n: Diocese of Hildesheim — Niewisch-Lennartz expert group on the Janssen era (2021)
who: Catholic Diocese of Hildesheim under Bishop Heinrich Maria Janssen
cover: Priests accused of abusing children were generally only moved to another parish; perpetrators got support and protection while victims got no help.
d: An external expert group led by former Lower Saxony justice minister Antje Niewisch-Lennartz, with former senior prosecutor Kurt Schrimm and the IPP institute, presented its report on 14 September 2021 on the tenure of Bishop Heinrich Maria Janssen (1957–1982). Its interviews identified 71 suspects, 45 of them clergy, the others lay staff, members of religious orders and youths in children's homes; 51 were active during Janssen's tenure. Accused priests were generally only transferred, in one case to South America, and children were left unprotected in tent camps, priests' homes and church children's homes. The group found no further evidence against Janssen himself but did not refute the two allegations made against him in 2015 and 2018. An earlier IPP study for the diocese appeared in 2017.

n: Diocese of Limburg — 'Betroffene hören – Missbrauch verhindern' project (2020)
who: Catholic Diocese of Limburg; bishops, vicars general and personnel directors
cover: The file review named diocesan leaders responsible for 'cover-up and silence' and found that protecting the institution guided decisions.
d: The Diocese of Limburg ran a project with about 70 mostly external experts from September 2019 to June 2020 as its response to the 2018 MHG study; the 415-page final report was presented on 13 June 2020 in Frankfurt's Paulskirche. Its file review covered 46 cases and found that diocesan leaders had played down the crimes and treated the accused as a threat to the clerical system rather than a danger to children. It named the leaders responsible for cover-up and silence and produced 61 measures against abuse. Survivors who took part criticised how little affected people were involved.

n: Redemptorists in Germany — interim reports (2010–2024) and IPP study (2026)
who: Redemptorist order in Germany — schools including the Collegium Josephinum, Bonn
d: Between 2010 and 2024 the Redemptorist order in Germany commissioned six interim reports on sexual violence, mainly at its schools. They documented at least 90 victims, mostly pupils, and at least 29 perpetrators from 1950 to 2011, including at the order's Collegium Josephinum grammar school in Bonn. In September 2026 the order presented a 276-page study by the Munich IPP institute (Heiner Keupp), commissioned jointly with survivors, on how it handled the cases from 2010.

n: Collegium Josephinum, Bad Münstereifel — Archdiocese of Cologne project report (2017)
who: Archdiocese of Cologne — Collegium Josephinum boarding school (closed 1997)
cover: The archdiocese, as operator, set no rules for educational methods and did not monitor practice.
d: A project led by educational scientist Claudia Bundschuh, with Bettina Janssen as operational lead and commissioned by the Archdiocese of Cologne, published its final report on 13 September 2017. About 100 former pupils described violence at the boarding school from at least the 1950s; the report found a 'system of abuse of power' up to at least the 1970s. Seven staff, all but one priests, were accused of sexual violence and twelve of physical violence. The archdiocese set no rules and did not supervise the school.

n: Bündnis 90/Die Grünen — review of paedophile advocacy in the party (2014–2016)
who: Bündnis 90/Die Grünen (federal party and Berlin branch); paedophile activist groups of the 1970s–80s
d: The Göttingen Institute for Democracy Research led by Franz Walter, commissioned by the Greens, presented its report in November 2014: paedophile activists got demands to legalise sex between adults and children into several Green resolutions in the 1980s, until a clear break at federal level in 1989, while in the Berlin branch the debate continued into the mid-1990s. A Berlin state-party commission reported in May 2015. The party's working group was contacted by 12 victims of child sexual abuse; three received payments for long-term abuse in the early 1980s in the Christian Emmaus community at Dachsberg in Kamp-Lintfort, where the party's institutional co-responsibility could not be ruled out. The party apologised in November 2014.

n: Tyrol and Vorarlberg — state-commissioned study of welfare and residential care (2015)
who: State welfare system and residential homes of Tyrol and Vorarlberg, incl. Jagdberg (Schlins), St. Martin (Schwaz), Mariatal (Kramsach), Kleinvolderberg
cover: The study found the institutional system produced, tolerated and failed to prevent physical, psychological and sexualised violence.
d: A University of Innsbruck team led by Michaela Ralser, commissioned by the state governments of Tyrol and Vorarlberg, presented its overall study of welfare and residential care on 6 July 2015. It examined four state institutions in detail (Jagdberg, St. Martin, Mariatal and Kleinvolderberg) and found a total institution of isolation and dependence that produced, tolerated and did not prevent physical, psychological and sexualised violence until the 1980s. By then 362 people in Tyrol and 159 in Vorarlberg had received compensation from the states since 2010.

n: SOS-Kinderdorf Austria — abuse at Imst and Moosburg, founder Hermann Gmeiner, and the Griss reform commission (2025–2026)
who: SOS-Kinderdorf Österreich — children's villages incl. Imst (Tyrol) and Moosburg (Carinthia); founder Hermann Gmeiner (died 1986)
cover: The allegations against Gmeiner were known internally for years (victims came forward 2013–2023) but were made public only in 2025.
d: After a Falter report in September 2025 on abuse by staff at Austrian SOS children's villages, SOS-Kinderdorf Österreich said on 23 October 2025 that there were credible allegations that its founder Hermann Gmeiner (died 1986) sexually and physically abused eight boys at four villages between the 1950s and 1980s; victims had come forward from 2013 and received compensation and therapy, but the organisation had not made this public. A later investigation report listed 16 suspected cases of sexualised violence by Gmeiner. An external reform commission chaired by former Supreme Court president Irmgard Griss presented its results on 25 June 2026, focusing on abuse at Moosburg and Imst, handling of earlier studies and possible cover-ups, and the lack of external oversight. Prosecutors in Klagenfurt, Innsbruck and Salzburg opened investigations.

n: Marist Brothers in Spain — independent commission recognises 25 victims (2020)
who: Marist Brothers (Hermanos Maristas) schools in Spain, incl. Barcelona
d: On 3 December 2020 the Marist congregation in Spain announced that an independent commission it had set up to review all cases had recognised 25 victims of sexual abuse by former teachers in its schools, with compensation reported at about 400,000 euros in total, including for time-barred cases. The Barcelona cases, from 1970 to 2010, were exposed by local press in 2016. Only one teacher, lay PE teacher Joaquín Benítez, was tried; in 2019 he was sentenced to 21 years and nine months for abusing four pupils, other complaints being time-barred.

n: Deetman Commission — supplementary inquiry into abuse of and violence against girls in the Catholic Church (2013)
who: Roman Catholic Church in the Netherlands — dioceses and religious orders
d: The Deetman Commission presented a supplementary inquiry on 11 March 2013 into sexual abuse of and violence against girls and young women who were minors in the Dutch Catholic Church from 1945 to 2012, after its 2011 report had found over 77% of identified victims were male. It received 79 new reports, of which 37 concerned only physical or psychological violence, and reconsidered 71 earlier reports of violence, 26 from women. It called on bishops and religious superiors to reach out to these victims; reports involving sexual abuse go to the Church's reporting point and compensation committees.

n: Latvia — Logos Centrs child exploitation network, Riga (1999–2002 convictions)
who: Logos Centrs video and model agency, Riga (director Jurijs Jurjevs)
d: After a September 1999 Latvian TV report, prosecutors investigated the Riga agency Logos Centrs, headed by Jurijs Jurjevs, which The Baltic Times described as a bogus modelling agency running a child pornography and prostitution ring; seven people were charged. Andris Meinarts was convicted on 21 counts of sexually abusing minors as a customer and sentenced to ten years, the maximum; pageant agency manager Ainārs Eisaks received 2.5 years; Ingus Tūns' case was tried separately. According to Wikipedia, citing Latvijas Vēstnesis and Delfi, 67 people, 61 of them minors, were sexually exploited, the agency had catalogued about 3,000 minors, Jurjevs received more than four years and Tūns five. Claims that senior politicians were clients were investigated and found false (see the Saeima commission record).

n: YMCA NSW — Royal Commission Case Study 2 (Caringbah childcare worker Jonathan Lord)
who: YMCA NSW (Caringbah out-of-school-hours care and holiday programmes)
d: The Royal Commission's first hearing (October 2013) examined how YMCA NSW and police responded to 2011 allegations that childcare worker Jonathan Lord sexually abused children in its care at Caringbah; Lord was convicted and jailed with a minimum term of six years. The commission heard he was hired after improper reference checks and that staff did not pass concerns to senior management. Its 165-page report, published 2 July 2014, found staff training insufficient and YMCA NSW's policies deficient, and said the case 'calls into question the child safety practices of YMCA NSW'.

n: Victoria — Board of Inquiry into historical child sexual abuse at Beaumaris Primary School and other government schools (2024)
who: Victorian Department of Education; Beaumaris Primary School and 23 other government schools
cover: Board found a culture of covering up child sexual abuse in the Department of Education to protect the system's reputation; a teacher convicted and found guilty of misconduct in the 1980s was moved into administration and banned from teaching for only three years
d: A Victorian Government Board of Inquiry, set up after reports of abuse at Beaumaris Primary School, tabled its final report in Parliament on 6 March 2024. It examined the school from 1960 to 1994 (abuse there was concentrated in 1971–72) and was widened to 23 other government schools. It focused on four teachers, out of six relevant staff, who are believed to have abused more than 100 students, mostly boys aged 9 to 12. The board found the department 'woefully failed to protect children', had no policies for handling allegations or convictions, and covered up abuse. It made nine recommendations, including a parliamentary apology and accountability processes for historical abuse in all state schools.

n: New Zealand — Confidential Listening and Assistance Service final report, 'Some memories never fade' (2015)
who: New Zealand state care: residential special education, health and welfare institutions
d: The New Zealand Government set up the Confidential Listening and Assistance Service, chaired by Judge Carolyn Henwood, in 2008 to hear people who had been abused or neglected in state care before 1992. It heard 1,103 participants and finished in June 2015; its final report, 'Some memories never fade', was released under the Official Information Act in August 2015. The panel described 'an alarming amount of abuse and neglect, with extreme levels of violence', including physical, sexual, emotional and verbal abuse, across the 50 years before 1992, and said much of it was preventable with better oversight.

n: IICSA — sexual abuse of children in custodial institutions, 2009–2017
who: Young offender institutions and secure training centres in England and Wales (incl. Medway and Rainsbrook STCs)
d: The Independent Inquiry into Child Sexual Abuse published its report on children in custodial institutions on 28 February 2019, after public hearings on 9–20 July 2018. It found that more than 1,000 incidents of alleged sexual abuse were reported in custody from 2009 to 2017, far more than official figures showed, and that children in young offender institutions and secure training centres remained at risk. Recent cases included staff touching detainees during searches and restraint; adult survivors also described abuse in custody decades earlier.

n: IICSA — Ealing Abbey and St Benedict's School (Benedictine)
who: Ealing Abbey (English Benedictine Congregation) and St Benedict's School
cover: IICSA found a culture of cover-up and denial; very senior figures at the school or abbey were perpetrators and staff were warned to say nothing; Abbot Martin Shipperlee's handling of allegations showed serious shortcomings.
d: IICSA's report of 24 October 2019 found abuse at St Benedict's School over more than 30 years, in a 'sadistic and predatory' atmosphere where harsh physical punishment often led to sexual abuse. Since 2003 four staff connected to the school had been convicted of offences against more than 20 children, and the inquiry received at least 18 further allegations against them and eight other monks and teachers. It found serious shortcomings in Abbot Martin Shipperlee's handling of allegations; he resigned during the investigation, saying some of the failings were his.

n: Scottish Child Abuse Inquiry — Keil School, Dumbarton
who: Keil School (closed 2000); Mackinnon-Macneill Trust
cover: After a parent complained early on about the physics teacher's behaviour, the problem was covered up by headmaster Christopher Tongue and other senior staff.
d: The fifteenth volume of findings, published 20 August 2025, found abusive practices normalised at Keil School from the late 1950s to the 1980s. Physics teacher William Bain (at Keil 1987–2000) sexually abused many children, some almost daily, after a parent's early complaint was covered up by the headmaster and senior staff; Bain was convicted in 2016 and again on 30 June 2025. An English teacher, David Gutteridge, was convicted in 2024 of abusing a pupil. Publication was delayed at the Crown's request until Bain's trial ended.

n: Scottish FA — Independent Review of Sexual Abuse in Scottish Football (2021)
who: Scottish football: Scottish FA and clubs including Celtic, Rangers and Hibernian (named among clubs asked to apologise)
d: The independent review chaired by Martin Henry, commissioned by the Scottish FA, published its final report on 11 February 2021, having been held back from 2018 until related criminal proceedings ended. It examined non-recent abuse mainly from the 1970s to the early 1990s and found that adults with a sexual interest in children moved easily through Scottish football and kept their activities hidden, with flawed decisions that sometimes meant little or no action. 33 people gave personal accounts; the review urged clubs including Celtic, Rangers and Hibernian to apologise publicly, and the Scottish FA apologised.

n: Clywch inquiry — Children's Commissioner for Wales on Ysgol Gyfun Rhydfelen
who: Ysgol Gyfun Rhydfelen (secondary school); Mid Glamorgan County Council education department
cover: In 1991 an education officer failed to make a child protection referral despite pupils' statements; the director of education obstructed a proper investigation, issued a misleading statement and let the teacher resign without action.
d: The first inquiry by the Children's Commissioner for Wales, Peter Clarke, published in 2004, concluded that drama teacher John Owen committed serious acts of sexual impropriety against pupils at Ysgol Gyfun Rhydfelen. Owen was charged in September 2001 after four former pupils went to police and was found dead in October 2001, before trial. The commissioner found that when sixth-formers complained in 1991 the Mid Glamorgan education officer made no child protection referral, and that the county's director of education obstructed a proper investigation and issued a misleading statement; Owen was allowed to resign without disciplinary action. It recommended independent school disciplinary tribunals for Wales and an independent children's counselling service.

n: Wanless–Whittam review — Home Office files on organised abuse claims (2014)
who: Home Office; Geoffrey Dickens MP's 1980s dossier; Paedophile Information Exchange funding claims
cover: 114 relevant Home Office files were missing, lost or destroyed; the review could not rule out that some were removed to hide abuse.
d: Peter Wanless and Richard Whittam QC reviewed, for the Home Secretary, how the Home Office handled information about organised child abuse in the 1980s, including Geoffrey Dickens MP's dossier.
