Their report, submitted 15 October 2014 and published 11 November 2014, found no evidence of an organised Home Office effort to hide child abuse, but said 114 files were missing, lost or destroyed and the imperfect records meant removal to hide abuse could not be ruled out. It found nothing to support claims that the Home Office funded the Paedophile Information Exchange.

n: House of Commons Home Affairs Committee — child sexual exploitation and localised grooming (2013)
who: Police, social services and the Crown Prosecution Service; Rochdale and Rotherham councils
d: The Home Affairs Committee's report of 10 June 2013 (HC 68-I) found that police, social services and the Crown Prosecution Service had failed vulnerable children in some areas and that this was still happening across the country. It found Rochdale and Rotherham councils slow to recognise organised abuse of children, many in council care, and blamed a lack of professional curiosity. It described a model of localised grooming involving mainly Pakistani-heritage men targeting young white girls but warned against focusing on that model alone, and recommended court reforms.

n: Church of England — second Past Cases Review (PCR2, 2022)
who: Church of England dioceses, cathedrals and national institutions
cover: Allegations were often handled informally, without investigation, records or referral to safeguarding professionals.
d: The Church of England's second Past Cases Review, reported nationally on 5 October 2022, examined more than 75,000 files, some from the 1940s, and identified 383 new cases: 168 involved children, 149 vulnerable adults and 27 both. 242 cases involved clergy, 53 other church officers and 41 volunteers working with children. It found allegations had often been handled informally without proper investigation or referral, and made 26 national recommendations. The archbishops apologised.

n: Madonna House residential centre, Dublin — Department of Health inquiry (1996)
who: Madonna House children's residential centre, run by the Sisters of Charity
cover: Management failed to act on staff concerns and children's complaints; one staff member regarded as having an inappropriate relationship with a girl was paid to live elsewhere but kept his job; the sections describing abuse were removed from the published 1996 report and only revealed in 1999.
d: The report of the inquiry into Madonna House, a Sisters of Charity residential centre for children in Dublin, was published in 1996 with its most damaging sections removed on legal advice. The withheld sections, revealed in May 1999 after RTÉ's States of Fear team obtained them, described beatings, humiliation and sexual assaults on children by a small number of staff, and management that failed to take effective action on staff concerns and children's complaints.

n: Iceland — Catholic Church investigative commission on Landakotsskóli (2012)
who: Catholic Church in Iceland; Landakotsskóli school and church summer camps
cover: The commission reported that Bishop Joannes Gijsen destroyed a letter from a man who said the priest had abused him.
d: An investigative commission of the Catholic Church in Iceland, chaired by Hjördís Hákonardóttir, reported in early November 2012. It confirmed that Rev. Ágúst Georg, principal of the church's Landakotsskóli school, and teacher Margrét Müller abused pupils. Of 30 former pupils and summer-camp children questioned, 8 said they had been sexually abused and 27 described mental abuse. It found that Bishop Joannes Gijsen destroyed a letter reporting abuse by the priest. In December 2015 the Althing passed Act No. 117/2015, extending the state compensation scheme for abuse in institutions to Landakotsskóli.

n: Bolivia — two former Jesuit provincials convicted for not reporting Fr Alfonso Pedrajas (2025)
who: Society of Jesus (Jesuits), Bolivian province
cover: The court found the provincials knew of allegations against Pedrajas and did not report them to police; prosecutors seized internal Jesuit documents in La Paz and Cochabamba in May 2023
d: On 2 September 2025 a Bolivian court sentenced Marcos Recolons and Ramón Alaix, Jesuit provincials of Bolivia in 1993–1999 and 1999–2007, to one year in prison each, plus costs, compensation to victims and psychological treatment, for knowing of allegations against Fr Alfonso Pedrajas and not reporting them. Pedrajas, who died in 2009, wrote in a diary published by El País in 2023 that he abused at least 85 minors between 1972 and 2000. Prosecutors presented 18 victims' complaints and 34 witnesses and said they would pursue other priests named at trial. Sentences under three years are normally commuted in Bolivia.

n: Nepal — Hague Conference mission finds regular falsification of papers to make children 'adoptable' (2010)
who: Child-care homes and intermediaries in Nepal's intercountry adoption system; foreign adoption agencies
d: At the request of Nepal's Ministry of Women, Children and Social Welfare, the Permanent Bureau of the Hague Conference on Private International Law sent a technical assistance mission to Nepal on 23–27 November 2009; its report is dated 4 February 2010. It cited evidence that documents were regularly falsified to declare children adoptable, with false statements about abandonment, origin, age and status, and that this continued under the 2008 rules. It said the USD 5,000 per-child payment and USD 10,000 annual agency fee created strong incentives unrelated to the cost of care, and that Nepal had no data on adoptable children.

n: Brazil — Senate 'CPI da Pedofilia' on online abuse material and child abuse (2008–2010)
who: Users of the Orkut social network and offenders across Brazil; the CPI's hearings were credited with the fall of a Pará state deputy, Luiz Afonso Sefer, convicted at first instance in 2010
d: The Federal Senate's parliamentary inquiry into paedophilia, chaired by Senator Magno Malta, worked for almost three years, the longest CPI to date, and its rapporteur Demóstenes Torres handed a final report of nearly 1,700 pages to police and prosecutors in December 2010. It signed a conduct agreement with Google, the Federal Police and prosecutors to lift secrecy on Orkut pages linked to child sexual abuse. Rádio Senado reported that hundreds of people were arrested or indicted after its work, and Malta credited the CPI's hearings with the fall of Belém state deputy Luiz Afonso Sefer; Sefer was convicted in 2010 of raping a child, but the case has since been overturned, reinstated and annulled on appeal and, as of February 2026, his 20-year sentence had not been carried out. Laws passed during its work criminalised possession of child abuse material and ordered the closure of businesses where children were exploited.

n: Chile — Chamber of Deputies commission on irregular adoptions (2019)
who: Hospital medical and paramedical staff, Civil Registry staff, private intermediary organisations
cover: Some hospitals did not register or destroyed birth records from 1970 onward (e.g. Carlos Van Buren hospital, Valparaíso); the commission also found gaps in birth and departure records
d: A special investigating commission of the Chamber of Deputies, chaired by Deputy Boris Barrera, worked from January to 22 July 2019 on children taken from mainly poor, often rural mothers, some of whom were made to believe their babies had died, and given for adoption, many abroad, before, during and after the 1973–1990 dictatorship. It found complicity by medical and paramedical staff, Civil Registry staff and organisations operating outside hospitals, and noted that private intermediaries were paid for their role. It recommended an international DNA bank, a national truth commission on irregular adoptions and excluding private bodies from adoption; the Chamber approved the report on 4 October 2019 by 88 votes with 13 abstentions.

n: Colombia — Truth Commission volume on children: 16,238 recruited; recruited girls subjected to rape, forced contraception and abortion (2022)
who: FARC-EP, ELN and other guerrillas, paramilitary groups, and state security forces (recruitment and use of minors)
d: Colombia's Commission for the Clarification of Truth published its volume on children and adolescents, 'No es un mal menor', in July 2022. It documented 16,238 children recruited by armed groups between 1990 and 2017 and estimated the real number at 27,101 to 40,828, and described recruitment as intentional and systematic, including use of minors by the state security forces. It found that recruited girls were forced to use contraception at an early age, forced to have abortions, and subjected to harassment, rape and sexual torture.

n: South Africa — Human Rights Commission finds sexual abuse in schools systemic (2026)
place: Johannesburg (SAHRC); complaint from St John's College, Mthatha
who: Educators and other adults in South African schools; South African Council for Educators; education departments
cover: Professional deregistration of educators does not automatically lead to listing on the safeguarding register; a documented shortfall of 10,748 convicted offenders not yet entered on the National Register for Sex Offenders
d: After a complaint about alleged sexual violence by an educator at St John's College in Mthatha, Eastern Cape, the South African Human Rights Commission convened a stakeholder roundtable and on 29 June 2026 released a report describing sexual violence in schools as systemic and entrenched. It recorded 826 sexual misconduct complaints to the South African Council for Educators between 2021 and 2025 and found that professional deregistration does not automatically lead to inclusion on the safeguarding register, and that 10,748 convicted offenders had not yet been entered on the National Register for Sex Offenders.

n: Syria — UN Commission of Inquiry: rape of detained women, girls and boys; forced marriage of girls by ISIS (2018)
who: Syrian government forces and affiliated militias (worst offenders); Hay'at Tahrir al-Sham; Islamic State
d: The Independent International Commission of Inquiry on the Syrian Arab Republic released 'I lost my dignity' on 15 March 2018, based on 454 interviews covering March 2011 to December 2017. It found sexual and gender-based violence pervasive and committed by most parties: women and girls were raped in detention, at checkpoints and in house raids, and male detainees including boys were subjected to sexual torture, with government forces and allied militias named as the worst offenders. It found that Islamic State forced girls and women into marriages with its fighters, and that these acts amount to war crimes.

n: UN — Zeid report: 45% of 2004 peacekeeping SEA allegations involved sex with under-18s (2005)
place: Democratic Republic of the Congo (MONUC) and other missions; report issued at UN Headquarters, New York
who: UN peacekeeping military and civilian personnel
d: On 24 March 2005 the Secretary-General transmitted the report of his adviser Prince Zeid Ra'ad Zeid Al-Hussein on sexual exploitation and abuse in UN peacekeeping. Of 105 allegations recorded across missions in 2004, about 45% involved sex with persons under 18; in MONUC (DR Congo) 72 allegations were received between May and September 2004, and women interviewed described 'rape disguised as prostitution', with sex often costing about $1 to $3. OIOS considered 7 of the MONUC cases it examined fully substantiated and found convincing evidence in 2 more. The report recommended binding standards for all personnel, a professional investigative capacity, on-site courts martial and DNA paternity testing.

n: Freedom Hosting — Tor host for Lolita City and other abuse sites
who: Freedom Hosting (Eric Eoin Marques, convicted)
cover: Extradition from Ireland took from 2013 to 2019 through appeals.
d: Freedom Hosting was a free anonymous dark web hosting service that ran from July 2008 to July 2013 and hosted over 200 child exploitation websites, including Lolita City, which Anonymous had attacked in 2011. The operator, Eric Eoin Marques, was arrested in Dublin in early August 2013 on a US warrant; the FBI accused him of being 'the largest facilitator of child porn on the planet'. After Ireland's Supreme Court dismissed his challenge in March 2019 he was extradited, pleaded guilty on 6 February 2020 to conspiracy to advertise child sexual abuse material, and on 16 September 2021 was sentenced to 27 years. DOJ said the sites held millions of images and videos, over 1.97 million not previously known to law enforcement.

n: Operation Torpedo — FBI ran three Tor sites
who: Three Tor-hidden abuse sites run by a Nebraska man
d: Dutch police compromised one site and found it physically hosted at a Nebraska web host; the FBI found an employee running two sites at work and one at home. After a year of surveillance the FBI arrested him and operated the sites for two weeks, using a network investigative technique to reveal visitors' IP addresses. The US DOJ said in December 2015 that 18 US users had been convicted besides the operator; one was the acting cybersecurity director of the US Department of Health and Human Services.

n: Kidflix / Operation Stream
place: Bavaria (Bavarian State Criminal Police and ZCB)
who: Kidflix (paid streaming platform, 1.8 million users 2022–2025)
d: Kidflix, created in 2021, let users stream as well as download abuse videos, paying in cryptocurrency converted to tokens; 91,000 unique videos (6,288 hours) were uploaded. German and Dutch authorities seized the server on 11 March 2025, when it held about 72,000 videos. Operation Stream, led by Bavarian police with 38 countries and Europol, identified 1,393 suspects and arrested 79 during action weeks in March 2025; Europol called it the largest child sexual exploitation operation in its history.

n: South Korea school deepfake crisis on Telegram (2024)
who: Telegram group chats creating sexual deepfakes of classmates and teachers
d: In August 2024 a journalist's reporting revealed Telegram chatrooms, some dedicated to specific high schools and middle schools, where users made and shared sexual deepfakes of female students, teachers and others; one room for pupils at a single school had more than 2,000 members. Within a week activists had identified more than 500 schools and universities as targets. Police said they had handled more than 800 deepfake sex crime cases in 2024 by late September, against 156 in all of 2021, and that most victims and perpetrators were teenagers. On 26 September 2024 the National Assembly passed a bill criminalising possessing or watching sexual deepfakes; earlier that month police opened an investigation into whether Telegram was complicit.

n: Peter Scully — pay-per-view abuse streamed from Mindanao
who: 'No Limits Fun' dark web site (Peter Scully, Australian; Filipino accomplices)
d: An Australian from Melbourne who moved to Cagayan de Oro, Mindanao, in 2011 was alleged to have run a ring that abused children and sold videos of the abuse online to customers abroad. The Philippine investigation began with a tip from Dutch police, who found images on a seized hard drive. Arrested in 2015, he was charged with the murder of a 12-year-old girl as well as trafficking and child abuse. In June 2018 a Cagayan de Oro court sentenced him to life imprisonment after convicting him of one count of human trafficking and five counts of rape. On 3 November 2022, under a plea bargain, he was sentenced to a further 129 years; his former girlfriend, a co-accused, got 126 years and two others more than nine years each.

n: CVLT — neo-Nazi child exploitation group leaders arrested
who: CVLT (part of 'The Com')
d: On 30 January 2025 US HSI arrested two men for participating in CVLT, which groomed and coerced at least 16 minors worldwide into producing abuse material and self-harm imagery. Europol said earlier-arrested members included one in French custody since 2022 and one serving a 50-year US sentence. Europol describes these communities as part of 'The Com'.

n: US state lawsuits against Roblox and Discord over child exploitation (alleged)
place: Louisiana, Kentucky, Texas, Iowa, Tennessee, Indiana, Arkansas and others
who: Roblox Corporation; Discord Inc.
d: From 2025 US state attorneys general sued Roblox alleging it failed to protect children from predators, starting with Louisiana on 14 August 2025, whose attorney general called the platform 'the perfect place for pedophiles'; Kentucky, Texas, Iowa, Tennessee, Florida and Nebraska pursued similar claims, and in 2026 some states also sued Discord. In April 2026 Roblox began settling: Nevada (about $10–12 million), then Alabama ($12.2 million) and West Virginia ($11 million) on 21 April, with Roblox agreeing to age checks for all users by facial age estimation or government ID and other chat restrictions. These are allegations, not findings.

n: UK Online Safety Act 2023
who: UK Parliament / Ofcom
d: The Online Safety Act 2023 received royal assent on 26 October 2023. It provides for the regulation by Ofcom of certain internet services, including their handling of illegal content such as child sexual abuse material and content harmful to children. Its child-protection duties, including age checks for sites with certain adult content, came into force in late July 2025.

n: Grok image tool used to sexualise photos of minors (alleged)
who: X Corp / xAI (Grok)
d: After X rolled out an 'edit image' button for its Grok chatbot in late December 2025, users complained that it was being used to partially or completely remove clothing from pictures of women and children. On 2 January 2026 Grok posted that it had 'identified lapses in safeguards' and was 'urgently fixing them', adding that CSAM is illegal and prohibited; xAI replied to AFP with an automated message saying 'the mainstream media lies'. In August 2026 a plaintiff ('Jane Doe') sued, alleging Grok was trained on abuse material of her and that the Canadian Centre for Child Protection had found Grok-generated AI CSAM depicting her. NCMEC listed X.AI LLC among companies most of whose CyberTipline reports lacked enough information to locate offences, while noting improvements in early 2026. These are allegations.

n: Blue Orchid — Russian site selling abuse videos
who: Blue Orchid website
d: A Moscow-based website that sold videotapes of the sexual abuse of boys, some as young as 12, for $200 to $300 each, mostly mailed to customers in the United States. The investigation began in May 2000 when Moscow police asked the US Customs Service for help; Russian police arrested the alleged operators in December 2000 and the site was shut in January 2001. By 26 March 2001 US Customs announced that four US citizens and five Russians had been arrested, with customers arrested in California, New York and Indiana and leads passed to Sweden, Denmark and the Netherlands.

n: Project Spade — Azov Films, Toronto
who: Azov Films (Toronto distributor of 'naturist' films of children)
cover: Germany's BKA received the customer list in October 2011 but began investigating only in October 2012; a German MP on the list later resigned, and information about the case was passed to his party leader.
d: Toronto police undercover officers made contact with a man sharing graphic abuse images in October 2010, which led to Azov Films, a Toronto company run by Brian Way that produced and sold films of child exploitation worldwide; after a joint investigation with the US Postal Inspection Service, police raided the business. Police said it was a $4 million business distributing to over 50 countries and seized over 45 terabytes of data. On 14 November 2013 Toronto police announced 348 arrests and 386 children rescued; those arrested included 40 school teachers, nine doctors and nurses, six law enforcement personnel, nine pastors and priests and three foster parents. Way was arrested in 2011 and in 2016 was found guilty of making and distributing child sexual abuse material and sentenced to ten years, reduced after a judge found he had been abused in jail.

n: Operation Gargamel — Belgian-led investigation of 9 million files
who: Offenders producing their own abuse material
d: Belgian federal judicial police found more than 9 million images and videos, mostly never seen before, in a house search. With Europol victim-identification taskforces, 90 suspects (24 in Belgium) and 110 victims were identified by March 2020; an Australian suspect was sentenced to 15 years. Police in over 40 countries received intelligence packages.

n: Operation Chemosh — minors sharing abuse 'stickers' in WhatsApp groups
who: Encrypted chat groups, many members minors
d: Begun in 2017 after a public report about children forming WhatsApp groups to create and exchange abuse material, including emoji 'stickers'. Thirty-three investigations were opened (26 in Spain) with arrests in Spain, Italy and France; the average age of those arrested in Spain was 22 because many were minors.

n: Operation Sky — Skype group sharing abuse material
who: Invitation-only Skype group with members from 14 countries
d: Spanish police followed Tor links to a private Skype group whose members from 14 countries exchanged abuse material; by May 2018 eight people had been arrested in France, Hungary, Italy, Spain and Canada.

n: Brazil orders Discord to suspend livestreaming (2026)
who: Discord Inc.
d: On 12 August 2026 Brazil's National Data Protection Authority (ANPD) ordered Discord to suspend its livestreaming feature nationwide, saying it had found 'robust evidence' that Discord failed to take reasonable steps to stop minors being exposed to content promoting violence, self-harm and suicide. The order followed the death in July 2026 of a 13-year-old girl in central-western Brazil who, authorities said, was encouraged during a Discord livestream to take her own life. Five teenagers were arrested in connection with her death, and police said the investigation also led them to another girl at risk, whom they reached in time. A Justice Ministry cyber-intelligence official called the case 'a terrible failure in moderation'.

n: Matthew Falder — dark web 'hurtcore' blackmailer
who: Individual offender posting on hurtcore dark web sites
cover: The NCA said technology companies' limited cooperation may have delayed identifying victims.
d: A Cambridge-educated Birmingham university researcher posed online as a depressed female artist to lure victims, some as young as 14, into sending images, then blackmailed them into sending increasingly degrading material, which he shared on dark web 'hurtcore' sites. The NCA estimated more than 50 victims between 2009 and 2017. A taskforce of the NCA, GCHQ, US Homeland Security Investigations, the Australian Federal Police and Europol, with police in Israel and Slovenia, identified him after four years; he was arrested in June 2017. He admitted 137 of 188 charges and was jailed for 32 years in February 2018, thought to be the first UK prosecution related to hurtcore material; in October 2018 the Court of Appeal reduced the sentence to 25 years.

n: Operation Protect Our Children — domain seizures (2011)
who: US ICE HSI
cover: Seizure of one shared domain redirected about 84,000 unrelated subdomains to a seizure warning.
d: In February 2011 ICE Homeland Security Investigations and the US Justice Department, under a court order obtained without notice to owners, seized about ten domain names alleged to be advertising or distributing child sexual abuse material. One seized domain belonged to a free shared DNS provider, so late on 11 February 2011 all 84,000 of its subdomains, mostly unrelated small websites, displayed the ICE seizure notice; the seizure was reversed within about two days.

n: Oxford — Operation Bullfinch and 2015 Serious Case Review
who: Grooming network; Thames Valley Police; Oxfordshire County Council
d: Seven men were jailed in May 2013 for a combined minimum of 95 years after Operation Bullfinch; the trial judge said police and social services missed tell-tale signs. The Oxfordshire Serious Case Review, published 3 March 2015, estimated that more than 350 young people were sexually exploited in the county from 1999 to 2014. It found police did not believe the girls and treated them as if they had chosen their situation, and social services knew of grooming but failed to protect them. Both the police and council apologised.

n: Derby — Operation Retriever
who: Grooming network; Derbyshire Police investigation
d: Derbyshire Police's Operation Retriever led to the conviction of nine men in 2010 for grooming and sexually abusing 26 girls, one aged 12. Thirteen men had been charged and eleven stood trial.

n: Casey national audit on group-based child sexual exploitation
who: Home Office; police forces in England and Wales
d: Baroness Casey's audit, published 16 June 2025, found that data flaws meant the scale of group-based exploitation could not be assessed, and that perpetrator ethnicity was not recorded for about two-thirds of cases. Local data from three police force areas showed 'disproportionate numbers of men from Asian ethnic backgrounds amongst suspects', which she said warranted further examination; she said flawed data had been used to dismiss concerns. The government accepted all 12 recommendations, including mandatory ethnicity and nationality data for suspects, charging adult sex with under-16s as rape, an NCA-led national operation, and a national inquiry with statutory powers.

n: Craigslist adult services closure (2010)
who: Craigslist
d: In September 2010 Craigslist removed its 'adult services' section from its US site, replacing it with a 'censored' label, after a letter from 18 state attorneys general led by Connecticut's Richard Blumenthal. The letter said the section carried rampant prostitution ads and facilitated human trafficking, including ads involving children. Blumenthal estimated the section could generate over $36 million in revenue. Much of the advertising later moved to Backpage, which AGs urged to close its own section that month.

n: Rendon-Reyes trafficking organization (Tenancingo)
who: Rendon-Reyes Trafficking Organization, Tenancingo, Tlaxcala
d: From December 2004 to November 2015 the Tenancingo-based Rendon-Reyes organization smuggled women and girls from Mexico and Central America into the US, forced them into prostitution and laundered proceeds back to Mexico. In January 2019 five members were sentenced in Brooklyn to between 15 and 25 years; others had pleaded guilty to racketeering and sex trafficking.

n: Australia — passport ban for registered child sex offenders (2017)
who: Australian Government
d: Laws taking effect on 13 December 2017 allow Australia to cancel the passports of up to 20,000 registered child sex offenders to stop them travelling to abuse children. The Foreign Minister said about 800 registered offenders travelled overseas in 2016, often to developing countries in Asia, and about 40% did so without notifying police. Reporting at the time said about half of the trips were to Southeast Asia.

n: Oba of Benin revokes trafficking 'juju' oaths (March 2018)
who: Oba of Benin, Ewuare II; Edo traditional priests
d: In March 2018 the Oba of Benin, Ewuare II, publicly revoked the curses that juju priests had used to bind trafficking victims to their traffickers and laid a curse on anyone involved in trafficking within his domain. Thomson Reuters Foundation reported in September 2018 that anecdotal evidence suggested trafficking had slowed, and cited UNODC that at least nine in ten Nigerian women trafficked to Europe come from Edo State.

n: Svay Pak child brothels — 2003 raid and later decline
who: Brothels in Svay Pak (mostly ethnic Vietnamese victims)
cover: The 22 January 2003 police raid was widely advertised in advance; almost all children had been moved and no pimps or clients were arrested. Local authorities had extorted brothel owners.
d: Svay Pak, a poor fishing village on the outskirts of Phnom Penh, became notorious as a place where foreign men bought sex with children; CNN in 2017 reported girls there being sold by their families. After crackdowns by the government, police and international agencies, open street sales ended and the trade moved to more hidden venues such as massage parlours and karaoke bars. ABC News reported in 2017 that survey estimates of the share of minors among Cambodia's sex workers had fallen from nearly 35% to 1–2%.

n: Kédougou, Senegal — sex trafficking of girls at gold-mining sites
who: Trafficking networks supplying mining camps
d: The 2025 US TIP report says traffickers exploit women and girls as young as 12 in sex trafficking throughout Senegal's southeastern gold-mining region of Kédougou; most victims are from Nigeria, with others from Senegal, Mali, Benin, Burkina Faso, Ghana, Guinea, Sierra Leone and China. It also reports some tourists exploit children in Dakar and Saint-Louis, and to a lesser extent Cap Skirring and La Petite Côte.

n: Madagascar — child sex tourism and karaoke-bar exploitation (US TIP 2025)
who: Malagasy and foreign offenders
cover: The report calls corruption and official complicity significant concerns; one official was investigated.
d: The 2025 US TIP report says most child sex-trafficking victims are exploited by Malagasy men, but foreign tourists, often from France, also exploit children; parents sometimes encourage daughters into commercial sex with tourists, and children are exploited in Antananarivo karaoke bars. Courts convicted 15 traffickers, the first convictions in four years. A Nosy Be anti-trafficking committee exists. In July 2025 police in Nosy Be arrested two women suspected of filming abuse of their own children and selling the videos to foreign buyers via mobile money (charged; L'Express de Madagascar).

n: Uganda — Karamojong children sold at border markets (US TIP 2025)
who: Traffickers including community 'elders'
d: The 2025 US TIP report says NGOs estimate the majority of child sex-trafficking victims in Uganda are ethnically Karamojong, especially from Napak district. Traffickers, sometimes community 'elders', force children to meet them at international borders, where markets are organized to sell children into domestic servitude or sex trafficking. Women, girls and boys are exploited in Kampala brothels, bars and homes.

n: DR Congo — forced labour and sexual exploitation of children at eastern artisanal mines (US TIP 2025)
who: Mining bosses, miners, family members, government officials, armed groups
cover: Traffickers named in the report include government officials; corruption and complicity contributed to impunity.
d: The 2025 US TIP report says mining bosses, other miners, family members, government officials and armed groups force or coerce adults and children into forced labour in artisanal mines in eastern DRC, including through debt bondage, and that most trafficking is internal, including sex trafficking and forced marriage of girls.

n: Nepal → India — trafficking of girls to Indian brothels (estimates)
who: Trafficking networks recruiting via false job, marriage and online romance offers
cover: US TIP 2025: serious concerns of official complicity; traffickers bribe some Indian officials to fly Nepali workers to third countries.
d: The 2025 US TIP report says traffickers use job offers and online romance scams to recruit Nepali women and children to India for sex trafficking; Nepali courts convicted 406 traffickers (231 for sex trafficking) in the year. A 2024 study it cites found a majority of workers in Nepal's adult entertainment sector were sex-trafficking victims, nearly half of them children. Research collated on Wikipedia gives estimates of 5,000–10,000 Nepali women and girls trafficked to India each year across a 1,850 km open border.

n: Pakistan → China — 629 girls and women sold as 'brides' (AP 2019)
who: Brokers selling poor (often Christian) Pakistani girls and women to Chinese men
cover: Officials told AP the investigation largely stopped after June 2019 because of pressure from government officials fearful of harming ties with Beijing; in October 2019 a Faisalabad court acquitted 31 Chinese nationals after witnesses were threatened or bribed into silence.
d: AP obtained a list compiled by Pakistan's Federal Investigation Agency of 629 girls and women sold as brides to Chinese men from 2018 to mid-2019. In October 2019 a court in Faisalabad acquitted 31 Chinese nationals charged in the biggest case. The 2025 US TIP report says traffickers target impoverished Christian communities to send women and girls to China, where hundreds reported being forced into commercial sex.

n: Mark Frost — 13 life terms for abuse of boys in Thailand and the UK (2017)
who: Mark Frost (also known as Andrew Tracey), former teacher and scout leader
d: Frost, who had held positions of trust in UK schools and scouting and first admitted an offence in 1992, abused boys from poor families in Thailand in 2011–2013, including streaming abuse by webcam to another European man. In February 2017 he was sentenced to 13 terms of life imprisonment after pleading guilty to 45 offences against boys in the UK and Thailand. The Independent Inquiry into Child Sexual Abuse cited the case as one of only about eight successful UK prosecutions since 1997 for offences committed abroad. Eight Thai boys secured civil compensation in 2018.

n: Indonesia — child sexual exploitation in the Riau Islands and 'contract marriages' in Puncak (US TIP 2025)
who: Foreign offenders; brokers of 'contract marriages'
cover: The report says the government tacitly accepted 'contract marriages'; corruption and complicity significantly impeded efforts.
d: The 2025 US TIP report says extraterritorial child sexual exploitation is prevalent in the Riau Islands bordering Singapore, and women and girls are coerced into commercial sex notably in Batam. It also reports that Middle Eastern tourists pay more than $700 for week-long 'contract marriages' in Puncak, Bogor, involving girls as young as nine, a practice the government tacitly accepted. In October 2017 Batam police arrested a Singaporean man accused of molesting three boys (IBTimes, charged).

n: Sri Lanka — child sex tourism in coastal areas (US TIP 2025)
who: Foreign and local offenders
d: The 2025 US TIP report says traffickers reportedly exploit boys and girls in child sex trafficking, including in coastal areas, for foreign offenders, and recommends investigating complicit establishments. The government convicted six traffickers and identified seven child victims in the year.

n: Colombia — Tren de Aragua sex trafficking of Venezuelan girls; webcam industry (US TIP 2025)
who: Tren de Aragua; ELN; webcam studios
cover: Two complicit officials received plea-deal sentences of 7.5 years, below the statutory minimum.
d: The 2025 US TIP report says Tren de Aragua and the ELN run sex-trafficking networks in Villa del Rosario, Norte de Santander, and Tren de Aragua uses Cúcuta's transport hub to move victims to Argentina, Ecuador and Peru and operates in Bogotá, Cali, Medellín and Pereira. Traffickers recruit women and girls, mostly Colombians and displaced Venezuelans, into 'webcam modelling', an industry likely worth over $1.2 billion a year. Sex trafficking of girls is prevalent in tourist areas and extractive zones.

n: Brazil — Federal Highway Police 'Projeto Mapear' of child sexual exploitation points on highways
who: Truck stops, bars, motels along federal highways
d: Brazil's Federal Highway Police (PRF) and Childhood Brasil have mapped roadside sites vulnerable to child sexual exploitation for about 19 years. The 2021–2022 survey, released 31 May 2023, assessed more than 9,700 points, rating 640 critical and about 1,800 high-risk; the worst conditions were on BR-116 (12 critical points), BR-153, BR-101, BR-163, BR-232 and BR-040. An earlier edition found 69% of victims female and 22% transgender, and 38% from elsewhere, possibly trafficked. The 2025 US TIP report says child sex trafficking is common along BR-386, BR-116 and BR-255.

n: Haiti — restavek child domestic servitude and gang exploitation of children (US TIP 2025)
who: Host families (restavek); armed gangs
cover: Observers report police and immigration officials complicit at the Haiti–Dominican Republic border.
d: The 2025 US TIP report says a large share of Haiti's trafficking cases involve children in restavek domestic servitude, often physically abused and unpaid, and that displacement from Port-au-Prince increased children's risk of sexual exploitation in the restavek system. Gangs exploit women and girls in sex trafficking; an international organization reported close to 50 per cent of gang members are children, with a 70 per cent rise in child recruitment in 2024.

n: Europol: at least 10,000 unaccompanied migrant children missing in Europe (2016)
who: Europol; organized crime exploiting the migrant flow
d: On 31 January 2016 Europol's chief of staff Brian Donald told The Observer that at least 10,000 unaccompanied children had disappeared after arriving in Europe, 5,000 of them in Italy and 1,000 in Sweden, and that Europol had evidence some had been sexually exploited. He said an entire criminal infrastructure had developed over 18 months around exploiting the migrant flow, with many arrests in Germany and Hungary. Save the Children estimated 26,000 unaccompanied children arrived in 2015.

n: Bulgaria — girls trafficked to Western Europe; exploitation in state institutions (US TIP 2025)
who: Traffickers; Roma forced marriages to third-country nationals
cover: Corruption in law enforcement and the judiciary and impunity for complicit officials were pervasive; 34 convicted traffickers received suspended sentences.
d: The 2025 US TIP report says traffickers exploit Bulgarian women and girls in sex trafficking throughout Western Europe and in Sofia, resort areas and border towns, and cites a UN special rapporteur finding that child sexual exploitation, including potential sex trafficking, was prevalent among children in government-run institutions. Courts convicted 31 traffickers; only eight received custodial sentences.

n: UK — 5,999 child potential victims referred to the National Referral Mechanism (2024)
who: Home Office (NRM)
d: Home Office statistics show 19,125 potential victims of modern slavery referred in 2024, 31 per cent (5,999) children; 78 per cent of child referrals were boys and criminal exploitation was the most common type (48 per cent). UK nationals were 23 per cent of all referrals, three-quarters of them children; Vietnamese nationals were 11 per cent, 416 of them children. In 2017 the Times reported more than 150 Vietnamese minors had gone missing from UK care since 2015.

n: Jordan and Türkiye — Syrian refugee girls in forced marriages and sex trafficking (US TIP 2025)
who: Families and brokers arranging unofficial marriages
cover: Türkiye: no investigations of complicit officials reported, though corruption and complicity remained significant concerns.
d: The 2025 US TIP report says Syrian girls in Türkiye — which hosted about 2.9 million displaced Syrians — are forced into marriages in unofficial religious ceremonies, particularly in poor rural regions, and then subjected to domestic servitude and sex trafficking. In Jordan, Syrian refugee women and girls have been sold into forced marriages, and in 2022 authorities investigated a mother for allegedly exploiting her two daughters with foreign tourists.

n: ECPAT 'Offenders on the Move' — Global Study on Sexual Exploitation of Children in Travel and Tourism (2016)
who: ECPAT International and partners (High-Level Task Force chaired by Najat Maalla M'jid)
d: Published 12 May 2016 after two years' work, the study found sexual exploitation of children in travel and tourism had grown despite 20 years of effort, as international arrivals rose from 527 million to 1.135 billion a year. It found there is no typical offender: most are domestic or regional travellers and 'situational' offenders rather than Western paedophiles; the internet has opened new pathways; and conviction rates are alarmingly low. It identified the US and Canada as source countries for offenders and Europe as a source, with exploitation rising in Central and Eastern Europe.

n: Colombia — Constitutional Court orders Medellín archdiocese to release priests' files
who: Archdiocese of Medellín; Salesian Inspectorate of San Luis Beltrán, Medellín
cover: Both the archdiocese and the Salesian province refused journalist Juan Pablo Barrientos's 2019 request for the records of 43 priests, calling them private; the archdiocese appealed the first-instance ruling against it.
d: In May 2019 journalist Juan Pablo Barrientos, author of 'Dejad que los niños vengan a mí', asked the Archdiocese of Medellín and the Salesians for the records of 43 priests, including complaints against them. After both refused, he filed tutela actions. On 3 March 2020 the Constitutional Court ruled that the information was semi-private and that the right to information prevailed, ordering the archdiocese to hand it over. In 2022 the Court agreed to review a further petition covering 915 priests who served in Medellín.

n: Puerto Rico — Arecibo priests defrocked; island-wide probe
who: Diocese of Arecibo; at least four Puerto Rican dioceses
cover: Prosecutor Yolanda Pitino said the diocese's information was insufficient and it had not answered requests for more; Justice Secretary César Miranda warned he might charge church officials suspected of withholding information.
d: In early 2014, after reports in El Nuevo Día, Bishop Daniel Fernández disclosed that since 2011 he had expelled six priests accused of sexual abuse in the Arecibo diocese. Local prosecutors said at least 11 other priests on the island were under investigation, and the Justice Secretary said at least four dioceses were being investigated. U.S. Homeland Security Investigations requested information.

n: Bob Jones University — GRACE report
who: Bob Jones University (independent fundamentalist Christian)
cover: Several victims said campus counselors did not report their abuse to legal authorities; counseling blamed victims and treated all 'sexual sin' as equal. The university fired and then rehired GRACE during the investigation.
d: Bob Jones University hired GRACE (Godly Response to Abuse in the Christian Environment) in November 2012 to review its handling of sexual abuse. GRACE's roughly 300-page report, released 11 December 2014, found the school responded to abuse claims with ignorance of state reporting law, little trauma training and a culture that blamed victims; some counselors encouraged victims to repent. The review was prompted in part by a board member's handling of a 1997 case in which a minor girl raped by a church deacon in New Hampshire was made to confess before the congregation. The university president apologised.

n: Thailand — Chiang Dao monks arrested for procuring a boy for an abbot
who: Temple in Chiang Dao (Theravada Buddhist)
d: On 19 June 2013 Chiang Mai police arrested two young monks, aged 20 and 23, accused of repeatedly taking a 14-year-old boy to a temple abbot for sexual services since February. Police said the two faced up to 15 years in jail; the abbot had not yet been arrested pending a warrant.

n: Amish bishop pleads guilty to failure to report (Dauphin County)
place: Mifflin Township / Elizabethville, Dauphin County, Pennsylvania
who: Amish church district, Dauphin County
cover: Told of two abuse cases in 2011, the bishop did not report them and told police he had been told one 'wasn't really that bad'.
d: Amish bishop Christ M. Stoltzfus, 70, pleaded guilty in Dauphin County court in September 2017 to failure to report child abuse and received three months' probation. A church member had told him in 2011 about two cases of child sexual abuse by another member; state police began investigating in January 2017 after a confidential tip.

n: Ferns Report — Diocese of Ferns
who: Catholic Diocese of Ferns
cover: Bishop Herlihy moved accused priests to other posts or dioceses for a period, then reinstated them; Gardaí failed to record or properly investigate some pre-1988 complaints
d: The state Ferns Inquiry, published 25 October 2005, examined more than 100 allegations of child sexual abuse made between 1962 and 2002 against 21 priests of the diocese. Bishop Donal Herlihy moved accused priests temporarily and then reinstated them, and ordained men he knew or should have known posed a risk. Bishop Brendan Comiskey never got a priest to stand aside from ministry. The report found Garda handling of one of eight formal complaints 'wholly inadequate' and some pre-1988 complaints were not recorded.

n: Scoping Inquiry — abuse in religious-run schools
who: 42 religious orders that ran day and boarding schools
d: The state Scoping Inquiry, published 3 September 2024, recorded 2,395 allegations of sexual abuse against 884 alleged abusers at 308 schools run by 42 religious orders, mostly from the 1960s to the 1990s. 590 allegations involving 190 alleged abusers concerned 17 special schools. More than half of the alleged abusers are dead. The government announced a full Commission of Investigation.

n: John Jay College study — US Catholic clergy 1950–2002
place: United States (commissioned by US bishops, Washington DC)
who: US Conference of Catholic Bishops (commissioned study)
cover: Of accused priests whose cases reached police, only one in three was charged; 3% served prison time
d: The John Jay College of Criminal Justice study, commissioned by the US bishops and released 27 February 2004, counted 4,392 priests and deacons (about 4% of clergy) accused of abusing 10,667 minors between 1950 and 2002. Reported abuse peaked in the 1970s; one-third of allegations were made only in 2002–03. 149 priests with more than 10 allegations each accounted for 27% of allegations. Costs to the church were put at $472 million at the time.

n: Archdiocese of Agaña — Archbishop Apuron and bankruptcy
who: Archdiocese of Agaña; former Archbishop Anthony Apuron
d: A Vatican tribunal of the Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith found former Archbishop Anthony Apuron guilty of some charges including sexual abuse of minors in March 2018; the appeal was rejected in February 2019. He was barred from office and from living in Guam but not laicised; he denies the allegations. The archdiocese filed for bankruptcy in January 2019 facing more than 200 lawsuits naming 35 clergy, teachers and scoutmasters. Guam lifted the civil statute of limitations in 2016.

n: Royal Commission into Abuse in Care — Catholic institutions
who: Catholic Church in Aotearoa New Zealand; St John of God Brothers at Marylands School
cover: Church relied on psychiatrists' opinions to transfer abusers to other ministries where they reoffended; commission recommended investigating priests transferred to Papua New Guinea
d: The Royal Commission's final report, Whanaketia, published 24 July 2024, found about 200,000 people were abused in state and faith-based care from 1950 to 2019. It found Catholic responses inadequate, noting a 2020 church briefing that 14% of clergy were accused over 1950–1999, and singled out Marylands School in Christchurch for some of the highest levels of sexual abuse. It found abusers were transferred to other ministries and recommended an inquiry into priests sent to Papua New Guinea.

n: Deetman Commission — Catholic Church in the Netherlands
who: Catholic dioceses and religious orders in the Netherlands
cover: Policy of 'not hanging out the dirty washing'; bishops and officials knew and did not act
d: The commission led by former minister Wim Deetman, set up by the church in March 2010, reported on 16 December 2011. It identified at least 800 priests, monks and other religious who abused children between 1945 and 1985, 105 of them still alive, and estimated tens of thousands of victims. It found bishops and officials knew of the abuse and followed a policy of avoiding scandal.

n: Peter Hullermann — transferred from Essen to Munich 1980
who: Archdiocese of Munich and Freising; Diocese of Essen
cover: Accused priest accepted into Munich for therapy in January 1980 with Cardinal Ratzinger's approval, then reassigned to pastoral work where he abused again; remained a priest until 2010
d: In January 1980 the Munich archdiocese under Cardinal Joseph Ratzinger agreed to receive Fr Peter Hullermann from the Diocese of Essen for therapy after he had been suspended there over abuse of a boy. He was then given pastoral work, abused minors again, and in June 1986 was convicted, fined 4,000 marks and given an 18-month suspended sentence with five years' probation. He kept serving in Bavarian parishes until the archdiocese suspended him in March 2010. Then vicar general Gerhard Gruber took 'full responsibility' for letting him back into pastoral work.

n: CIASE (Sauvé Commission) — Catholic Church in France
who: Catholic Church in France (commissioned by bishops and religious orders)
cover: Commission called the abuse 'massive' and 'systemic' and said the church must accept institutional responsibility
d: The Independent Commission on Sexual Abuse in the Church, chaired by Jean-Marc Sauvé, reported on 5 October 2021. Using a population survey, it estimated about 216,000 people were abused as minors by clergy and religious from 1950 to 2020, and about 330,000 including lay people working in church institutions. Archive research put the number of abusive clergy and religious at 2,900 to 3,200, a floor of 2.5% to 2.8% of the roughly 115,000 who served, and it described the abuse as massive and its causes as systemic.

n: Independent Commission — Catholic Church in Portugal
who: Catholic Church in Portugal (commission set up by the bishops)
d: An independent commission set up by the Portuguese church and led by child psychiatrist Pedro Strecht reported on 13 February 2023, after hearing from more than 500 survivors, that at least 4,815 children had been abused in the church since 1950. Most offences were time-barred; 25 cases were passed to prosecutors.

n: Fernando Karadima, Bishop Barros and Chile's bishops' resignation offer
who: Archdiocese of Santiago; Fr Fernando Karadima; Bishop Juan Barros; Cardinals Errázuriz and Ezzati
cover: Parishioners reported Karadima to Archbishop Fresno in 1984; Cardinal Errázuriz shelved a credible 2004–05 investigation; Barros, a Karadima protégé, made bishop of Osorno in 2015
d: The Vatican found Fr Fernando Karadima guilty of sexual abuse in 2011 and sentenced him to a life of prayer and penance; Pope Francis dismissed him from the priesthood on 27 September 2018, announced the next day. Four of his protégés became bishops, including Juan Barros of Osorno, whom Francis had defended. After receiving a 2,300-page report from Archbishop Charles Scicluna, Francis wrote in April 2018 that he had been mistaken in his assessment of the situation in Chile. Every bishop in Chile offered to resign in May 2018; by the end of June five resignations, including Barros's (11 June), had been accepted. In October 2018 an appeals court found the Archdiocese of Santiago liable for covering up for Karadima in a suit by three survivors naming Cardinals Errázuriz and Ezzati.

n: Mexican bishops' conference — 426 priests investigated
who: Conferencia del Episcopado Mexicano
cover: El Universal reported only six convictions out of 156 alleged abuse cases involving minors, 2009–2019
d: On 14 January 2020 the Mexican Episcopal Conference said it was investigating 426 priests over the previous ten years: 271 cases of abuse of minors in church settings and 155 other proceedings. It said 217 priests had been removed from their duties. El Universal reported in February 2020 that prosecutors had opened 156 investigations into such sexual offences by religious figures from 2009 to 2019, but four prosecutors' offices recorded only six sentences.

n: UN Committee on the Rights of the Child — Holy See review (2014)
who: Holy See
cover: Committee found abusive clergy were reassigned without police notification, bishops not required to report to civil authorities, and a code of silence
d: On 5 February 2014 the UN Committee on the Rights of the Child said it was gravely concerned that the Holy See had not acknowledged the extent of the crimes, had not taken the necessary measures against child sexual abuse, and had adopted policies that allowed abuse to continue. It said the Holy See had consistently placed the church's reputation and the protection of perpetrators above children's best interests, accused it of transferring abusive priests to new parishes, urged it to require clergy to report abuse to police, and criticised a 'code of silence' under which whistleblowers were ostracised, demoted and fired.

n: McCarrick Report (Holy See, November 2020)
who: Holy See; former Cardinal Theodore McCarrick
cover: A 1999 warning letter reached Pope John Paul II; an inquiry stalled after three of four US bishops gave 'inaccurate and incomplete information'; McCarrick was promoted to Washington in 2000
d: The Holy See's report of 10 November 2020 found that Pope John Paul II appointed Theodore McCarrick Archbishop of Washington in 2000 despite a letter from Cardinal John O'Connor dated 28 October 1999 warning that the appointment would risk serious scandal, and after McCarrick denied the allegations. Benedict XVI did not order an investigation but had McCarrick told to retire in 2006 and keep a lower profile, which he did not do. The report said Francis did not learn that McCarrick was accused of abusing a minor until 2017. On 11 January 2019 the CDF found him guilty of solicitation in confession and sexual offences with minors and adults, and he was dismissed from the priesthood (announced 16 February 2019). A Massachusetts charge of assaulting a 16-year-old at a 1974 wedding reception was dismissed on 30 August 2023 after he was found incompetent to stand trial because of dementia. He died in April 2025.

n: Diocese of Raphoe — Fr Eugene Greene
who: Catholic Diocese of Raphoe
d: Fr Eugene Greene, the most notorious offender in the Diocese of Raphoe, was sentenced in 1999 to 12 years in prison for abusing 26 boys over 20 years. A church safeguarding review published on 30 November 2011 found allegations against 14 Raphoe priests between 1975 and 2010, four of whom had been convicted, and pointed to 'significant errors of judgement' by successive bishops. Former bishop Séamus Hegarty said his past practice was 'sometimes poor' and apologised.

n: Scottish Child Abuse Inquiry — Fort Augustus Abbey and Carlekemp (Benedictines)
who: English Benedictine Congregation — Fort Augustus Abbey School and Carlekemp Priory School
cover: Complaints to senior monks were inadequately handled; after one complaint the school did not tell police and sent the monk, Denis Chrysostom Alexander, back to Australia
d: On 11 August 2021 Lady Smith published the Scottish Child Abuse Inquiry's findings on residential care run by the Benedictine monks of Fort Augustus Abbey between 1948 and 1991, concluding that children at Carlekemp Priory School, North Berwick, and Fort Augustus Abbey School suffered sexual, physical and emotional abuse; 43 witnesses gave evidence in 2019. A 2013 BBC investigation had presented evidence against seven Fort Augustus monks. Denis Chrysostom Alexander, sent back to Australia after parents complained, was arrested in Sydney in 2017, returned to Scotland in January 2020, pleaded guilty in June 2021 to abusing two boys and was jailed for four years and five months. Robert MacKenzie was extradited from Canada in 2020 but the case was dropped in 2021.

n: Basilian Fathers — Canadian convictions
who: Congregation of St. Basil (Basilian Fathers)
d: Basilian priest William Hodgson Marshall pleaded guilty in 2011 to 16 counts of indecent assault and one of sexual assault from 1952–1986 in Windsor, Toronto and Sudbury schools. Robert Whyte pleaded guilty in 1990 to abusing 18 children (1962–1982); Kenneth O'Keefe received house arrest in 2012–2013. In April 2020 the Supreme Court of Canada let stand an award of over $2.5 million, including $500,000 punitive damages, against the Basilians.

n: Diocese of Lafayette — Gilbert Gauthe (first national case)
who: Diocese of Lafayette; Fr Gilbert Gauthe
cover: Bishop assigned him as Boy Scout chaplain in 1974 despite allegations; sent for therapy in 1976 and returned
d: Fr Gilbert Gauthe admitted abusing 37 children while serving in the Diocese of Lafayette from 1972 to 1983. In 1974 the bishop made him a Boy Scout chaplain despite allegations about altar boys. In October 1985 he pleaded guilty and was sentenced to 20 years; the diocese paid more than $20 million. His 1984–85 case was the first widely publicised clergy abuse prosecution in the US.

n: Marist Brothers in Australia
who: Marist Brothers
cover: Royal Commission found the order failed to act on complaints against a Brother at Marist College Ashgrove; a Brother pleaded guilty in 2020 to concealing abuse
d: Data presented to the Royal Commission in February 2017 showed that 20% of Marist Brothers in Australia between 1950 and 2010 had been the subject of child sexual abuse allegations. Brother William Wade, a former headmaster at Marist schools in Canberra, Hamilton (Newcastle) and Kogarah, was jailed for 18 months in 2017 for abusing two boys (in 1976 and about 1980). In February 2020 he became the first senior Catholic in Australia to plead guilty to concealing child sexual abuse by colleagues, and in September 2020 was sentenced to four months, served in the community. The Marist Brothers listed 154 members accused of abusing children in June 2019.

n: Richard Daschbach — Topu Honis shelter, Oecusse
who: Society of the Divine Word (SVD); US-born Fr Richard Daschbach
d: US-born Divine Word missionary Richard Daschbach founded the Topu Honis children's shelter in Oecusse in 1992. After a complaint to his superiors in February 2018 he admitted the abuse to them in March 2018, and the Vatican dismissed him from the priesthood on 6 November 2018; the church did not tell the public. He was arrested in April 2019 and charged with 14 counts of sexually abusing children under 14, plus child abuse material and domestic violence counts. On 21 December 2021 a court in Oecusse sentenced him to 12 years, basing the verdict on the testimony of four victims. A report by the Dili archdiocese's Justice and Peace Commission had defended him.

n: Croatia — first priest convictions
who: Catholic dioceses in Croatia
cover: Nediljko Ivanov, whose abuse 1983–1991 was reported in 2012, was time-barred; a church court ordered only prayer, fasting and an apology and he continued to say Mass
d: In 2000 Fr Ivan Čuček was convicted of abusing 37 girls; his three-year sentence was cut to 18 months by the Supreme Court. In 2007 Fr Drago Ljubičić of Rab became the first Croatian priest to serve prison time, three years for molesting five teenage boys. Fr Nediljko Ivanov of Bibinje became the first priest convicted by a Croatian church court, but civil prosecution was time-barred.

n: Italy — no national inquiry; Rete l'Abuso count
who: Catholic Church in Italy; Italian Bishops' Conference
cover: In May 2012 the Italian Bishops' Conference said priests had no obligation to report suspected abuse to police
d: Italy has no official statistics or national inquiry. The victims' network Rete l'Abuso counted about 300 cases of priests and nuns before Italian courts since 2000, with 150 to 170 convictions (October 2018). In May 2012 the Italian Bishops' Conference said its priests had no duty to report suspected abuse to police. Cases include Fr Mauro Galli (6 years 4 months, 2014) and a former Roman Rota judge who pleaded guilty to child abuse image offences in 2018.

n: Diocese of Chichester — clergy abuse (IICSA case study)
who: Church of England, Diocese of Chichester
cover: Clergy with known concerns (Rideout, Cotton, Graves, House) were given or kept permission to officiate; Cotton's prior conviction for indecent exposure involving a child sat in his diocesan file but was not shared with police; an archdeacon declined to report a serious indecent assault; Sussex Police dropped a 1997–98 investigation and later destroyed its records.
d: IICSA found the Diocese of Chichester had more child sexual abuse convictions than any other Church of England diocese. Roy Cotton had been ordained in the 1960s despite a prior conviction involving a child. Sussex Police investigated Cotton and Colin Pritchard in 1997–98 without charges; when Northamptonshire Police revived the case in 2006, Sussex Police had destroyed its records. The diocese's 2008–09 Past Cases Review missed the scale of abuse, and real action against abusers began only with Operation Perry in 2011.

n: Canada residential schools run by Anglican, United and Presbyterian churches
who: Anglican Church of Canada (ran over 30 schools), United Church, Presbyterian Church, with the Catholic Church and federal government
cover: The schools were a federal government system run by churches.
d: Canada's Indian residential schools were run for the federal government by the Anglican, Catholic, Presbyterian and United churches; the Anglican Church of Canada operated more than 30. In April 2013 Truth and Reconciliation Commission chair Justice Murray Sinclair said about 37,000 former students had filed claims for sexual abuse, serious physical abuse or other wrongful acts, and asked the public to imagine 'a school where half of the students suffered sexual and physical abuse'. The TRC's final report followed in 2015. Under the 2006 Indian Residential Schools Settlement Agreement, to which the Anglican, Presbyterian and United churches were parties (Anglicans ran about 30% of schools, the United Church about 10%), the Independent Assessment Process for sexual and serious physical abuse had paid C$3.18 billion to 31,103 former students by 31 March 2019 (all churches combined).

n: ForuM study — German Protestant Church (EKD)
place: EKD, Hanover (all regional churches and Diakonie)
who: Evangelische Kirche in Deutschland (EKD) and Diakonie
cover: Researchers said regional churches delivered documents slowly despite a contract, so the study could not be completed; co-author Martin Wazlawik called the figures 'the tip of the tip of the iceberg'.
d: The ForuM study, commissioned by the EKD in 2020 and led by Hanover University of Applied Sciences and Arts, was released on 25 January 2024. Files reviewed showed 2,225 victims and 1,259 potential perpetrators among ministers, employees and volunteers since 1946, with a projected estimate of up to 9,355 abused minors. EKD head Kirsten Fehrs called it a 'massive failure' toward victims.

n: Bountiful, B.C. — parents convicted of taking 13-year-old to marry Warren Jeffs
who: FLDS, Bountiful community
d: In February 2017 a B.C. Supreme Court judge in Cranbrook convicted Brandon James Blackmore and Emily Gail Blackmore of removing a child from Canada for sexual purposes: in 2004 they took their 13-year-old daughter to the Utah–Arizona line to be married to Warren Jeffs, then 48. Both were jailed in August 2017. In the same trial James Oler was acquitted of a related charge.

n: Charity Commission inquiry — Manchester New Moston Jehovah's Witnesses congregation
who: Manchester New Moston Congregation of Jehovah's Witnesses (charity); Watch Tower Bible and Tract Society of Britain
cover: Trustees dismissed one allegation as a matter between two teenagers, did not enforce restrictions on the accused, and the victims were effectively required to repeat their allegations at an internal hearing in front of the abuser, who was allowed to question them. The charity did not give the Commission accurate and complete answers. The Watch Tower Society fought the inquiry through five courts and tribunals until 2016.
d: Allegations of child abuse against a trustee of the New Moston congregation were made in 2012 and 2013; he was later convicted of two counts of indecent assault. The Charity Commission opened a statutory inquiry on 27 May 2014 and published its report on 26 July 2017, finding the trustees had not adequately dealt with the allegations. The Commission also ran a wider inquiry into the Watch Tower Bible and Tract Society of Britain.

n: Latter-day Saints abuse help line — Bisbee, Arizona case (AP investigation)
who: The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints
cover: After the father confessed to his bishop, the bishop called the church's abuse help line; church lawyers told him the clergy-penitent privilege meant he had to keep it secret. AP reported the abuse continued for about seven years afterwards. The help line, set up in 1995, routes calls that pose legal risk to church attorneys.
d: Paul Douglas Adams, a Border Patrol employee and church member in Bisbee, abused his daughter from age 5 and later a second daughter, and filmed the abuse; he stopped only when arrested in 2017 and died by suicide in jail before trial. An AP investigation published 4 August 2022 found church officials had known for years through confessions. Arizona law, like more than 20 states, lets clergy withhold abuse learned in confession. The church disputed the AP's account.

n: NXIVM — Keith Raniere convicted (including sexual exploitation of a 15-year-old)
who: NXIVM (self-help group run as a cult)
d: A Brooklyn federal jury convicted NXIVM leader Keith Raniere in June 2019 of racketeering, racketeering conspiracy, sex trafficking, attempted sex trafficking, forced labour conspiracy and wire fraud conspiracy. Prosecutors proved as racketeering acts that at 45 he sexually exploited a 15-year-old girl and photographed the abuse. On 27 October 2020 he was sentenced to 120 years and fined $1.75 million.

n: Nechemya Weberman — Satmar counsellor, Williamsburg
who: Satmar Hasidic community, Brooklyn
cover: During the case men were arrested for trying to bribe the victim and her husband to drop it; four were later convicted of coercion or witness tampering. Others photographed her on the witness stand and posted the images online.
d: Nechemya Weberman, an unlicensed counsellor in the Satmar community, abused a girl from age 12 to 15. He was convicted on all 59 counts on 10 December 2012 and sentenced on 22 January 2013 to 103 years, later cut on appeal. Brooklyn DA figures showed about 100 of 5,389 sex abuse cases since 2009 came from the Haredi community; critics said DA Charles Hynes's policy of not naming Haredi defendants protected the community.

n: Anglican Diocese of Brisbane — Archbishop Peter Hollingworth's handling of abuse
who: Anglican Diocese of Brisbane; Toowoomba Preparatory School; Church of England Boys' Society
cover: A diocesan inquiry found that in 1993 Archbishop Hollingworth allowed a known paedophile to keep working as a priest. He later became Governor-General of Australia.
d: Peter Hollingworth was Anglican Archbishop of Brisbane from 1989 to 2001 and became Governor-General in June 2001. In December 2001 he faced allegations that he had handled sexual abuse cases poorly as archbishop. His successor, Phillip Aspinall, set up a church inquiry in February 2002 into the handling of nine abuse cases; its report was tabled in the Queensland Parliament on 1 May 2003, and Aspinall said Hollingworth had made a 'grave and serious' error of judgement. Hollingworth announced his resignation as Governor-General on 25 May 2003.

n: Dilworth School — Anglican boarding school, Auckland
who: Dilworth Trust (Anglican-linked school for boys from disadvantaged families)
cover: The independent inquiry concluded that ongoing silence about the abuse was 'the primary reason for the damage' to former students.
d: Police arrested and charged six men on 14 September 2020 over offences at Dilworth alleged to date from the 1970s to the early 2000s. An independent inquiry led by Dame Silvia Cartwright and Frances Joychild KC, released on 18 September 2023 and covering 1950 to the present, found that sexual abuse was committed consistently from the mid-1950s to the end of 2005: 126 of 171 former students who gave information reported being sexually abused, and the inquiry knew of 49 more. Police estimated 233 student victims. The Royal Commission of Inquiry into Abuse in Care also examined Dilworth.

n: Samuel Bateman — FLDS splinter group, Short Creek
who: Splinter group of the FLDS led by Samuel Bateman
d: Samuel Bateman began claiming to be a new prophet in 2019 and led a group that broke off from the FLDS church. In a plea agreement he admitted 'spiritually marrying' 20 women and girls, 10 of them under age, with the intent of sexual activity with the girls. He was arrested in 2022, when nine child 'brides' were removed from homes. He pleaded guilty to conspiracy to transport a minor for criminal sexual activity and conspiracy to commit kidnapping, and on 9 December 2024 a federal judge in Phoenix sentenced him to 50 years. Two male followers who went to trial were convicted.

n: Lev Tahor — leaders convicted of kidnapping children
who: Lev Tahor (ultra-Orthodox sect)
d: In December 2018 Lev Tahor leaders Nachman Helbrans and Mayer Rosner took a 14-year-old girl and her 12-year-old brother in the night from their mother's home in upstate New York and moved them through several states to Mexico, where the girl was returned to the adult man the group had 'married' her to religiously at 13. The mother had fled the group's Guatemala compound in November 2018 and been granted sole custody. Both children were recovered in Mexico after three weeks. A federal jury convicted the two men in November 2021, and on 31 March 2022 each was sentenced to 12 years. Founder Shlomo Helbrans had been convicted in New York in 1994 of kidnapping a 13-year-old boy.

n: New Tribes Mission — Fanda boarding school, Senegal
who: New Tribes Mission (now Ethnos360)
d: A 2010 report by GRACE (Godly Response to Abuse in the Christian Environment), commissioned by New Tribes Mission after pressure from survivors, accused the mission of a culture of systemic abuse at the Fanda boarding school it ran in Senegal for missionaries' children, including sexual abuse of more than 20 children; a former dorm parent was identified as the most prolific perpetrator. 1992 field committee notes said allegations should not be reported to police. The mission then set up its own investigation process, IHART, to examine historical allegations at other schools.
